papers.title: How Low Can You Go: Fine-Tuning LLMs with Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO)
papers.summary: Recently, Morris et al. introduced TinyLoRA, a strategy for LLM fine-tuning which introduces arbitrarily few parameters, and demonstrated accuracy improvements using less than $10$ parameters rather than the ${\gtrsim 10,000}$ typically demanded by LoRA-based methods. However, that study continued to use gradient-based local search methods of the kind deployed for training multi-billion parameter LLMs in the first place. This article is predicated on the observation that, in the low dimensional setting, global optimization methods become tractable, unlocking Large language Model Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO). LlMBO is sample-efficient, gradient-free, memory-light, parallelizes across devices without synchronization, and, unlike policy-gradient methods, can optimize greedy-decoding accuracy directly. We describe numerical experiments comparing LlMBO against GRPO on fine-tuning tasks for a variety of models on a math benchmark suite which show that LlMBO can be a suitable alternative in this regime, matching or exceeding GRPO's fine tuning gains, while using a fraction of the compute and memory.

papers.title: Towards Safe Autonomy for Computer Use
papers.summary: The safety of LLM-based agents currently rests on alignment training and safety classifiers, neither of which can rule out that a sophisticated indirect prompt injection (IPI) goes through and causes significant harm. Recent work therefore builds agents with information-flow guarantees that rely on structured tool interfaces to interact with the environment. Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act visually on the computer screen, which does not provide a boundary between trusted first-party interfaces and untrusted, potentially attacker-authored content. Actions are equally ambiguous: a click may land on an application toolbar or a button controlled by an attacker. Treating the user as the source of trust and confirming each sensitive decision produces confirmation fatigue, with the risk of missing harmful actions. We introduce SA-CUA, a dual-LLM framework that generates a reliable trust boundary for CUAs by deriving conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree for unmasking trusted regions from the privileged LLM's screenshot, keeping trusted and untrusted content separated. Human interaction is only required for proper task specification in the beginning. During the task a robust endorsement channel allows values to pass from the untrusted to the trusted domain by verifying information via trusted channels. This allows the agent to autonomously handle tasks involving untrusted information. SA-CUA maintains much higher utility than CaMeL-CUA while keeping the attack success rate at zero.

papers.title: Beyond the Encoder: Object-Centric Representations Emerging from Segmentation Foundation Models
papers.summary: Foundation models are increasingly used as feature extractors for downstream tasks with limited data, typically through representations obtained from their encoders. However, foundation models trained for structured tasks such as segmentation also form object-specific representations during task execution, whose transferability remains largely unexplored. We investigate Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) object pointers, compact object-level representations produced through the segmentation pathway, as transferable representations for downstream tumour prediction. Through experiments on two PET/CT tumour prediction tasks, we find that object pointers learned using segmentation supervision alone already encode tumour-discriminative information, despite never being optimised for the downstream labels. We further introduce task-guided object pointers, where an auxiliary objective jointly shapes the object pointer space for the downstream prediction together with segmentation. Task-guided pointers improve cancer-type classification, outperforming conventional encoder-based transfer and radiomics, while segmentation-only pointers perform best on the more challenging recurrence prediction task. Representation analyses reveal associations between object pointers and interpretable radiomics features, class-dependent organisation of the learned representation space, and explicit spatial grounding around the segmented tumour. Together, these findings suggest that useful transferable representations can emerge through the execution of a foundation model's primary task, providing an alternative to conventional encoder-based transfer.

papers.title: Linear Last-Iterate Convergence Rates for Optimistic Learning in Harmonic Games
papers.summary: We prove that the last iterate of Optimistic Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (OFTRL) converges at a linear rate to a Nash equilibrium in multiplayer harmonic games. Our result holds under a mild game-regularity condition and for a large family of regularizers, including entropy, Tsallis, and log-barrier. Our analysis is based on a dual perspective of OFTRL: we prove that the interaction between optimism and the global structure of harmonic games leads to the dissipation of an energy function along the dual iterates, for which we establish tight quantitative bounds. Our result also holds for the Extragradient FTRL variant.

papers.title: Autonomous Cyber Operations Gym for Training and Evaluating AI Models for Defence
papers.summary: This paper proposes an Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) gym, a unified framework integrating high-fidelity network emulation, realistic user behaviour modelling for benign network traffic and adversarial profiles, and the generation of cybersecurity scenarios through open toolkits. By supporting live and deferred feature extraction at the packet and flow levels, the gym facilitates the creation of labelled synthetic datasets for training Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs), as well as developing and evaluating modular components for autonomous defence agents through emulated interactions. While evaluation of a DNN classifier within the gym shows high in-domain performance, achieving near-perfect recall on adversarial network flows, our experiments reveal a significant sensitivity to domain shift, showing that even minor changes in network composition, such as variations in traffic protocol distribution, can lead to a catastrophic collapse in model transferability and detection performance.

papers.title: Minimax rates for pointwise CATE estimation: the role of design smoothness
papers.summary: We study the role of design smoothness in the minimax estimation of conditional average treatment effects at a fixed covariate point. For design densities bounded above and away from zero, without further regularity, we derive upper and lower risk bounds with an arbitrarily small gap in the convergence-rate exponent. Under uniform design, we obtain matching upper and lower bounds at interior points in the regime of low nuisance smoothness. These results show that rough covariate designs can lead to slower rates than uniform designs, even under the same smoothness assumptions on the treatment effect and nuisance functions, highlighting the role of the covariate distribution in pointwise causal estimation.

papers.title: MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain, A Multi-Sensor, Multi-Temporal Pretraining Dataset for Earth Observation
papers.summary: Pretraining generalist Earth observation foundation models requires data that combine several sensors, varied temporal sampling and, increasingly, text, yet open datasets rarely provide all three in one consistent, easily accessible form. We introduce MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain, a collection of 279,166 tiles of 10 km drawn from the Major-TOM grid by clustering AlphaEarth embeddings. Each tile stacks Sentinel-2 L1C, Landsat-8/9, Sentinel-1 RTC, Copernicus DEM and ESA WorldCover on a shared 1056x1056-pixel, 10 m grid, complemented by cloud masks, OpenStreetMap entities and ERA5 weather. The tiles are partitioned into three temporal regimes, Monotemporal (250,000 tiles, one acquisition), Monthly (12,500 tiles, twelve acquisitions spread over the annual cycle) and Burst (16,666 tiles, six acquisitions within 30 days), and are released as 6.3 TB of Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs indexed by TACO v3 Parquet metadata, a standard that allows cloud streaming, efficient data access, and filtering before any pixel is read. A companion library derives sensor-tagged fact sheets, captions and 16 families of vision-language tasks from these layers at load time. We test our design choices in short pretraining runs of OlmoEarth-Base. First, a 25% subset of Major-TOM Core-S2L2A curated with AlphaEarth embeddings matches or exceeds the full corpus on 8 of 9 benchmarks. Second, on Elliot-Pretrain, adding Landsat-8/9 improves or matches Sentinel-2 only pretraining on every benchmark. Third, using DEM and WorldCover as prediction targets during pretraining further improves 8 of 9 benchmarks, while giving the same maps to the encoder as inputs degrades 5 of 9. Fourth, Sentinel-1 helps on 7 of 9 benchmarks, particularly on benchmarks with radar inputs. Fifth, rule-based captions match a small language model at no cost. The dataset is openly available at https://source.coop/major-tom/elliot-pretrain.

papers.title: Grid or Nodes? Probing Object Memory in World Models Under Partial Observability
papers.summary: A robot's world model must remember objects that leave the camera's view. FloWM, a learned world model, keeps them in a spatial grid of features that it moves with five built-in velocities. A node memory instead keeps each object's position and velocity as numbers. We compare them in FloWM's own block world, with an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as the node memory. How the grid is read changes its score: a single-cell probe finds 66% of out-of-view blocks, while FloWM's own probe 89%. FloWM also scores 8 points higher in view although no frame is shown, which we attribute to its write-back of its own predictions. Out of view, the tracker reaches FloWM's range in 14KB against 5.6MB, with no probe. On diagonal motion, outside its five velocities, FloWM finds 11% of blocks even after fine-tuning, while the unchanged tracker keeps 93%. Faster blocks defeat both until one more allowed speed takes the tracker to 94%, where FloWM's built-in shifts would need 25 copies of its grid. A learned node memory must still replace the oracles and handle velocity under noise, long gaps, and the bounce.

papers.title: Texture Interpolation as Texton Matching
papers.summary: Texture interpolation asks what should lie between two textures. Standard methods typically blend pixels or features at corresponding spatial locations, implicitly assuming that co-located elements should be mixed. For unrelated textures, however, this correspondence is arbitrary: a crack at one location has no particular relationship to a fiber at the same location in another image. We study whether this hidden pairing choice is itself a major determinant of interpolation quality. We represent textures as collections of local appearance vectors, or textons, and replace positional pairing with appearance-aware matching while keeping the encoder, representation, and decoder fixed. This isolates the effect of correspondence from changes in model capacity or training. Across texture pairs, appearance-aware matching consistently improves the distributional quality of interpolated midpoints over positional feature blending. Soft matching produces the strongest midpoint statistics, whereas one-to-one assignments yield more balanced transitions and closer agreement with the target endpoint. The same intervention also improves a second pretrained texture interpolator without retraining. These results identify correspondence as a first-class design choice in texture interpolation: meaningful transitions depend not only on how strongly two textures are mixed, but also on which local appearances are mixed with one another.

papers.title: On Collusion-Free Teaching in Planar Graphs
papers.summary: Non-clashing teaching minimizes teaching complexity among models satisfying the Goldman--Mathias collusion-avoidance criterion. While the Vapnik--Chervonenkis dimension (VCdim) measures the complexity of learning from samples, non-clashing teaching dimension (NCTD) measures the number of examples required when a teacher can select them. Whether NCTD is always bounded above by VCdim remains a fundamental open question in learning theory. In this paper, we investigate this question for the concept classes of closed neighborhoods in planar graphs. We prove a tight upper bound of two on their NCTD, thereby establishing the conjectured inequality for this family. For the positive variant NCTD+, in which teaching sets contain only positive examples, we obtain a tight upper bound of four. Finally, we show that deciding whether either NCTD+ or NCTD is at most one is NP-complete, even for concept classes of closed neighborhoods in planar graphs. In particular, despite the upper bound of two on NCTD for such classes, distinguishing between NCTD values of one and two remains NP-hard.

papers.title: AIRRI: Towards a Human-Readable, Machine-Resistant Reading Interface
papers.summary: The rapid advancement of image-to-text extraction systems and large language models (LLMs) poses new challenges for educational assessment by making assignment materials easy to transcribe and solve with minimal human effort. To address this problem, we present AIRRI (Artificial Intelligence Resilient Reading Interface), a framework for generating machine-resistant educational content, a dataset of higher-education assignments for evaluation, and an initial evaluation of the human readability of AIRRI machine-resistant text designs. AIRRI employs two categories of machine-resistance techniques. First, AIRRI applies image transformations including character spacing, word spacing, line spacing, character opacity variation, stripe overlays, and image noise. Second, AIRRI applies decision-based adversarial attacks: RayS, SurFree, and ADBA. We evaluate AIRRI against three image-to-text systems: Tesseract, EasyOCR, and the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our results show that AIRRI substantially degrades automated text extraction performance. AIRRI increased character error rates for EasyOCR (6.9% to 55.9%), Tesseract (2.3% to 100.0%), and GOT-OCR2 (30.7% to 48.1%). Word error rates increased for EasyOCR (24.9% to 96.7%) and Tesseract (10.7% to 100.0%). Among the evaluated decision-based attacks, ADBA consistently produced the largest degradation in image-to-text performance, while RayS and SurFree produced more moderate reductions. EasyOCR and Tesseract were generally more susceptible to both image-based and adversarial perturbations than the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our findings suggest that AIRRI can significantly reduce the reliability of image-to-text-to-LLM workflows, increasing the effort required for AI-assisted assignment completion.

papers.title: Emergent Loop Geometry in Gauge-Equivariant Graph Neural Networks
papers.summary: Gauge-equivariant graph neural networks generate ordered products of gauge links through local message passing, but the geometry of these internal structures is not captured by the receptive field alone. We investigate the statistical ensemble of closed lattice walks generated by recursive node- and edge-feature operations, independently of network training. Analytical and numerical results reveal a separation between rapid growth of contour length and much slower spatial expansion: deeper compositions generate increasingly long paths through repeated traversal of relatively compact regions. Loop expansions of fermionic observables provide a physical interpretation of this hierarchy, showing how spatial locality remains compatible with high-order dependence on nearby gauge fields. These findings identify complementary roles of network depth in extending spatial reach and enriching the representations constructed within that reach, providing a geometrical perspective on learning lattice gauge observables.

papers.title: Registration is a Representation Problem: Solving Whole-Body PET/CT Registration
papers.summary: Raw image intensities are a poor surrogate for similarity across images in correspondence problems. Further, while auxiliary segmentation labels can provide semantic identification and improve matching, they can assign only coarse identities to fine-grained anatomy and often cover only a subset of structures, particularly in whole-body settings. We present an approach that instead establishes correspondence using complementary representations of anatomy and demonstrate its utility for longitudinal whole-body PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg Challenge. Our 3D foundation model, anatomix, is used to derive fine-grained, per-voxel semantic representations that are consistent across volumes, and we further employ off-the-shelf segmentation models to obtain coarse anatomical identities. Together, these representations drive a GPU-accelerated iterative registration solver (FireANTs) in a hybrid multistage framework: the first stage estimates alignment from dense multi-channel features, after which a second refines the deformation using both anatomix- and segmentation-based losses. Lastly, because registration should not introduce non-biological tumor volume changes across time, we develop lesion-specific component-wise volume preservation schemes. Without any task-specific training, our system won first place in the PSMAReg Challenge leaderboard. Code and interactive visualizations are available at http://www.neeldey.com/reps-for-reg.

papers.title: Joint Neural Posterior Estimation and Model Selection for Chemical Reaction Networks
papers.summary: Simulation-based Bayesian inference for Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs) must simultaneously solve two computationally demanding problems: discriminating between overlapping reaction pathways and estimating reaction rate constants. Classical approaches, such as Sequential Monte Carlo ABC, rely on handcrafted summary statistics and scale poorly across large parameter spaces. To overcome this, we introduce a neural inference architecture. Our pipeline utilizes shared 1D-CNNs and a permutation-invariant Set Attention mechanism to learn low-dimensional summary statistics from variable-length, multi-experiment time-series data. These statistics simultaneously condition a model selection network to compute posterior model probabilities and model-specific conditional Invertible Neural Networks (cINNs) that estimate parameter posterior distributions. We demonstrate the practical utility of our approach on a real protodeboronation example, illustrating how it handles structural ambiguity and extracts kinetic parameters from competing catalyst deactivation pathways.

papers.title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories
papers.summary: Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density. Importance-weighted formulations of this identity yield a consistent target throughout training, while unweighted variants define a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme. We benchmark the different approaches in two-dimensional \(\phi^4\) theory and identify effective choices that enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Ultimately, our data-free training approach achieves comparable performance to training on HMC reference data.

papers.title: Cepheid: Decoupling Scale from Structure for Cross-Family Motion Completion
papers.summary: Sparse-to-dense motion completion recovers dense mesh motion from sparse vertex displacements. Residual priors trained on one geometry family frequently fail to beat parameter-free harmonic extension off-family. Moreover, cross-family training meets a scaling barrier: residual amplitude varies by more than an order of magnitude across geometry families and collapses as observations become denser. Since this scale depends on unknown target motion, it cannot be measured directly at test time. We decouple residual structure from physical scale by learning a dimensionless prior, estimating amplitude from observables and a lightweight correction fitted only on training sources. Our unified model surpasses harmonic extension across all evaluated families, including unseen cloth and legged bodies, without skeletons, registration, or cross-mesh correspondence. The same prior applies without retraining to point-tracked animal video and a robot grasping a soft body. Project page: https://su-terry.github.io/cepheid-website/

papers.title: Efficient Constrained Graph Search for Post-hoc Error Correction in Binary Classifiers
papers.summary: This study develops a graph search algorithm to find the optimal discrimination path for the binary classification problem. The objective function is defined as the difference of variations between the true positive (TP) and false positive (FP). It uses the depth first search (DFS) algorithm to find the top-down paths for discrimination. It proposes a dynamic optimization procedure to optimize TP at the upper levels and then reduce FP at the lower levels. To accelerate computing speed while improving accuracy, it proposes a reduced histogram algorithm with variable bin size instead of looping over all data points to find the feature threshold of discrimination. The algorithm is applied on top of a Support Vector Machine (SVM) model for a binary classification problem on whether a person is fit or unfit. It significantly improves TP and reduces FP of the SVM results (e.g., reduced FP by 90\% with a loss of only 5\% TP). The graph search auto-generates 39 ranked discrimination paths within 9 seconds on an input of 328,464 objects, using a dual-core laptop computer with a processor of 2.59 GHz.

papers.title: The Geometry of the Set of Equivalent Linear Neural Networks
papers.summary: We characterize the geometry of the set of all weight vectors for which a fully-connected linear neural network computes the same linear transformation $W$. Said another way, the set of all sequences of matrices (of predetermined sizes) whose product is $W$. This set of weight vectors is an algebraic variety in the Euclidean weight space, called the fiber of $W$ under the matrix multiplication map. Sometimes this variety is a manifold, but usually not. The rank stratification of a fiber is a natural partition of the fiber into smooth manifolds of various dimensions called strata. We derive the dimensions of these strata and characterize how they are connected to each other. They satisfy the frontier condition: if a stratum intersects the closure of another stratum, then the former stratum is a subset of the closure of the latter stratum. This subset relationship can be expressed as a partial order with a single minimal element, a stratum that is included in the closure of every other stratum. Hence the strata can be arranged in a hierarchy represented by a directed acyclic graph that represents that partial order; we give an algorithm that computes that graph. A key result describes the relationship between this partial order and the ranks of certain matrices in the network. We derive the tangent and normal subspaces of the strata, and we construct elegant bases for those subspaces. Each stratum represents a different pattern of information flow through the network, expressed as a barcode, borrowed from the study of persistent homology. The topology of a stratum depends solely on its barcode. So does its geometry, up to a linear transformation in weight space. Connections among the strata are best understood through "barcode moves," which can be expressed as simple modifications of the barcodes.

papers.title: Transductive Off-policy Proximal Policy Optimization
papers.summary: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is a popular model-free reinforcement learning algorithm, esteemed for its simplicity and efficacy. However, due to its inherent on-policy nature, its proficiency in harnessing data from disparate policies is constrained. This paper introduces a novel off-policy extension to the original PPO method, christened Transductive Off-policy PPO (ToPPO). Herein, we provide theoretical justification for incorporating off-policy data in PPO training and prudent guidelines for its safe application. Our contribution includes a novel formulation of the policy improvement lower bound for prospective policies derived from off-policy data, accompanied by a computationally efficient mechanism to optimize this bound, underpinned by assurances of monotonic improvement. Comprehensive experimental results across six representative tasks underscore ToPPO's promising performance.

papers.title: Convergence of Sharpness-Aware Minimization Algorithms using Increasing Batch Size and Decaying Learning Rate
papers.summary: The sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) algorithm and its variants, including gap guided SAM (GSAM), have been successful at improving the generalization capability of deep neural network models by finding flat local minima of the empirical loss in training. Meanwhile, it has been shown theoretically and practically that increasing the batch size or decaying the learning rate avoids sharp local minima of the empirical loss. In this paper, we consider the GSAM algorithm with increasing batch sizes or decaying learning rates, such as cosine annealing or linear learning rate, and theoretically show its convergence. Moreover, we numerically compare SAM (GSAM) with and without an increasing batch size and conclude that using an increasing batch size { achieves a lower worst-case $\ell_\infty$ adaptive sharpness} than compared with using a constant batch size and learning rate.

papers.title: Generative Conformal Prediction with Optimized Coverage Allocation
papers.summary: Conformal prediction provides model-agnostic uncertainty quantification with guaranteed coverage, but conventional methods often yield overly conservative uncertainty sets, particularly in multimodal or heterogeneous settings. This inefficiency arises from two sources: (i) limited expressiveness of the predictive model and (ii) simplistic nonconformity score design. Most existing approaches advance only one of these axes, leaving the other underexplored. We propose generative conformal prediction with Optimized Ranking and Coverage Allocation (ORCA), a three-stage framework that advances both aspects jointly. ORCA leverages generative models to capture the full conditional distribution and introduces a rank-dependent optimization procedure that adaptively allocates coverage for efficiency while maintaining validity. We cast this coverage allocation as an optimization problem, derive an exact mixed-integer linear programming formulation, and show that the solution converges asymptotically to the oracle density-level set. Across synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real datasets, ORCA produces substantially more efficient uncertainty sets than state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating robust gains in scenarios where conventional conformal prediction methods fail.

papers.title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data via APIs 3: Using Simulators Instead of Foundation Model
papers.summary: Differentially private (DP) synthetic data enables the use of sensitive datasets while providing strong privacy guarantees. Recently, Private Evolution (PE) has emerged as a promising framework for generating DP synthetic data using only inference APIs of foundation models. However, suitable foundation models are not always available for every private data domain. In this paper, we show that PE is more general than previously understood and can incorporate APIs beyond foundation models. In particular, we show that state-of-the-art non-neural-network data synthesizers, including computer graphics-based image generators and physics simulation tools (which we refer to as simulators), integrate naturally into PE. We call the resulting method Sim-PE. Sim-PE broadens the applicability of PE while improving performance. For image synthesis, Sim-PE improves downstream classification accuracy by up to 3x, reduces FID by up to 80%, and is significantly more efficient. We further show that simulators and foundation models can be seamlessly combined within Sim-PE for additional gains. Beyond performance improvements, Sim-PE enables new DP applications that are difficult or impossible for existing methods, including generating DP control signals whose execution reproduces the distribution of private observations. The code is open-sourced in the Private Evolution Python library: https://github.com/microsoft/DPSDA

papers.title: Sublinear Algorithms for Wasserstein and Total Variation Distances: Applications to Fairness and Privacy Auditing
papers.summary: Resource-efficiently computing representations of probability distributions and the distances between them while only having access to the samples is a fundamental and useful problem across mathematical sciences. In this paper, we propose a generic framework to learn the probability and cumulative distribution functions (PDFs and CDFs) of a sub-Weibull, i.e. almost any light- or heavy-tailed, distribution while the samples from it arrive in a stream. The idea is to reduce these problems into estimating the frequency of an appropriately chosen subset of the support of a properly discretised distribution. We leverage this reduction to compute mergeable summaries of distributions from the stream of samples while requiring only sublinear space relative to the number of observed samples. This allows us to estimate Wasserstein and Total Variation (TV) distances between any two distributions while samples arrive in streams and from multiple sources. Our algorithms significantly improves on the existing methods for distance estimation incurring super-linear time and linear space complexities, and further extend the mergeable summaries framework to continuous distributions with possibly infinite support. Our results are tight with respect to the existing lower bounds for bounded discrete distributions. In addition, we leverage our proposed estimators of Wasserstein and TV distances to tightly audit the fairness and privacy of algorithms. We empirically demonstrate the efficiency of proposed algorithms across synthetic and real-world datasets.

papers.title: Asynchronous Sharpness-Aware Minimization For Fast and Accurate Deep Learning
papers.summary: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) is an optimization method that improves the generalization performance of machine learning models. Despite its effectiveness, it has not been widely adopted in real-world applications due to its high computational cost. Existing approaches reduce this overhead by approximating or reusing gradients in the perturbation step, but still assume sequential perturbation and update steps. In this study, we introduce AsyncSAM, a variant of SAM that enables concurrent model perturbation and parameter updates across multiple compute resources. By adjusting the perturbation batch size in a system-aware manner, our asynchronous scheme fully overlaps perturbation with updates, eliminating the overhead and allowing even CPUs to perform perturbations without extra time. We also provide theoretical analysis showing that AsyncSAM achieves the same order of convergence as conventional SAM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AsyncSAM delivers superior generalization performance and the highest training throughput among state-of-the-art SAM variants. For example, in ViT fine-tuning on CIFAR-100, it achieves accuracy comparable to SAM while maintaining training time nearly identical to SGD.

papers.title: Weisfeiler and Leman Follow the Arrow of Time: Expressive Power of Message Passing in Temporal Event Graphs
papers.summary: An important characteristic of temporal graphs is how the directed arrow of time influences their causal topology, i.e., which nodes can possibly influence each other causally via time-respecting paths. The resulting patterns are often neglected by temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs). To formally analyze the expressive power of TGNNs, we lack a generalization of graph isomorphism to temporal graphs that fully captures their causal topology. Addressing this gap, we introduce the notion of consistent event graph isomorphism, which utilizes a time-unfolded representation of time-respecting paths in temporal graphs. We compare this definition with existing notions of temporal graph isomorphisms. We illustrate and highlight the advantages of our approach and develop a temporal generalization of the Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm to heuristically distinguish non-isomorphic temporal graphs. Building on this theoretical foundation, we derive a novel message passing scheme for temporal graph neural networks that operates on the event graph representation of temporal graphs. An experimental evaluation shows that our approach performs well in a temporal graph classification experiment.

papers.title: The Serial Scaling Hypothesis
papers.summary: While machine learning has advanced through massive parallelization, we identify a critical blind spot: some problems are fundamentally sequential. These "inherently serial" problems-from mathematical reasoning to physical simulations to sequential decision-making-require sequentially dependent computational steps that cannot be efficiently parallelized. We formalize this distinction in complexity theory, and demonstrate that current parallel-centric architectures face fundamental limitations on such tasks. Then, we show for first time that diffusion models despite their sequential nature are incapable of solving inherently serial problems. We argue that recognizing the serial nature of computation holds profound implications on machine learning, model design, and hardware development.

papers.title: Understanding the Interplay between Memorization and Learning in Large Language Models
papers.summary: We investigate foundational questions about the interplay between memorization and learning in large language models (LLMs). When an LLM generates a string, can we disentangle the roles of rote memorization and contextual learning? Rote memorization results in an LLM regurgitating specific details of a training string, while contextual learning leads to the generation of new strings that follow generalizable patterns of the underlying language. Related questions of interest include: can an LLM avoid memorization when optimally learning a language?, and if not, can we design training schemes to reduce memorization and improve learning? To address these questions, we propose contextual memorization, a new measure that precisely disentangles memorization from learning. Using this measure, we establish that different training strings are memorized at different epochs in training, and that memorization of some training strings is unavoidable when optimally learning a language. Finally, we propose memorization-aware training, a scheme that dynamically down-samples training strings based on their memorization, and in doing so, equalizes learning across strings, reduces memorization, and improves learning. Our conclusions are supported by extensive experiments on multiple LLMs using formal languages as a controlled testbed, enabling precise language specification, exact string sampling, and elimination of data contamination; and further validated on natural languages.

papers.title: Inexact calculus of variations on the hyperspherical tangent bundle with connections to the attention mechanism
papers.summary: We offer a theoretical mathematical background through Lagrangian optimization on the unit hyperspherical manifold and its tangential structure. Our methods can be categorized as inexact since our methods are projection-based and since we will perturb the functional optimization with epsilon-type quantities. We draw connections to the attention mechanism and the Transformer since it exists as a flow map in the tangent fiber for each token along the high-dimensional unit sphere. Our motivation for this work is primarily twofold: we study the attention mechanism under its flow map and its relations to traditional calculus of variations and Lagrangian optimization; and we study several calculus problems of variations on the unit hypersphere that appeal to a broader mathematical lens in approximating, variational contexts.

papers.title: PVD-ONet: A Multi-scale Neural Operator Method for Singularly Perturbed Boundary Layer Problems
papers.summary: Physics-informed neural networks and physics-informed DeepONet excel at solving partial differential equations but often struggle with singularly perturbed problems. To address this limitation, we propose two novel data-free frameworks: the Prandtl--Van Dyke neural network(PVD-Net) and its operator-learning extension, the Prandtl--Van Dyke Deep Operator Network(PVD-ONet). Each framework provides leading-order and high-order versions to meet different modeling requirements. The leading-order PVD-Net integrates Prandtl's matching condition for improved stability, while the high-order PVD-Net employs Van Dyke's matching principle to capture fine-scale boundary layer structures with higher accuracy. Extending PVD-Net to operator learning, PVD-ONet enables efficient prediction for families of boundary layer problems without retraining. Numerical experiments on representative one- and two-dimensional problems demonstrate that the proposed methods outperform existing baselines. Beyond forward prediction, the framework also supports inverse problems by inferring the scaling exponent governing boundary layer thickness from sparse observations, highlighting its potential for practical applications.

papers.title: Signature-Kernel One-Class Learning with Manifold Regularisation for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.summary: One-class learning is an effective methodology for time series anomaly detection, yet kernel one-class approaches often compare sequences in a pointwise fashion and ignore the geometry of normal data. In this work, we present a manifold-regularised, large-margin $\ell_p$-support vector data description ($\ell_p$-SVDD) method that analyses sequences as paths via the signature kernel. By incorporating a a graph-Laplacian penalty into the $\ell_p$-SVDD objective function and utilising the representer theorem for manifold regularisation, we illustrate that the dual task retains the functional form of the original one with a modified kernel matrix. As such, existing Frank--Wolfe solvers can be applied unchanged. We show that this new modified kernel is a valid kernel matrix and under a generic norm bound on the discriminant, the proposed model yields a smaller Rademacher-complexity bound than the baseline. Furthermore, the signature kernel which is computed through a Goursat partial differential equation and can handle irregularly sampled data and is invariant to reparametrisation has not previously been used for one-class time series anomaly detection to the best of our knowledge. Our experiments on five widely used benchmarks, evaluated without point adjustment, demonstrate that the proposed approach compares very favourably with the state of the art approaches.

papers.title: Cross-Subject and Cross-Montage EEG Transfer Learning via Individual Tangent Space Alignment and Spatial-Riemannian Feature Fusion
papers.summary: Personalised music-based interventions offer a powerful means of supporting motor rehabilitation by dynamically tailoring auditory stimuli to provide external timekeeping cues, modulate affective states, and stabilise gait patterns. Generalisable Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) thus hold promise for adapting these interventions across individuals. However, inter-subject variability in EEG signals, further compounded by movement-induced artefacts and motor planning differences, hinders the generalisability of BCIs and results in lengthy calibration processes. We propose Individual Tangent Space Alignment (ITSA), a novel pre-alignment strategy incorporating subject-specific recentering, distribution matching, and supervised rotational alignment to enhance cross-subject generalisation. Our hybrid architecture fuses Regularised Common Spatial Patterns (RCSP) with Riemannian geometry in parallel and sequential configurations, improving class separability while maintaining the geometric structure of covariance matrices for robust statistical computation. Using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, `ITSA' demonstrates significant performance improvements across subjects and conditions. The parallel fusion approach shows the greatest enhancement over its sequential counterpart, with robust performance maintained across varying data conditions and electrode configurations. The code will be made publicly available at the time of publication.

papers.title: A Note on Graphon-Signal Analysis of Graph Neural Networks
papers.summary: A recent paper, ``A Graphon-Signal Analysis of Graph Neural Networks'', by Levie, analyzed message passing graph neural networks (MPNNs) by embedding the input space of MPNNs, i.e., attributed graphs (graph-signals), into a space of attributed graphons (graphon-signals). Based on extensions of standard results in graphon analysis to graphon-signals, the paper proved a generalization bound and a sampling lemma for MPNNs. However, there are some missing ingredients in that paper, limiting its applicability in practical settings of graph machine learning. In the current paper, we introduce several refinements and extensions to existing results that address these shortcomings. In detail, 1) we extend the main results in the paper to graphon-signals with multidimensional signals (rather than 1D signals), 2) we extend the Lipschitz continuity to MPNNs with readout with respect to cut distance (rather than MPNNs without readout with respect to cut metric), 3) we improve the generalization bound by utilizing robustness-type generalization bounds, and 4) we extend the analysis to non-symmetric graphons and kernels.

papers.title: Bouncy particle sampler with infinite exchanging parallel tempering
papers.summary: Markov chain Monte Carlo is one of the most useful tools for obtaining samples from complex distributions, such as posterior distributions in Bayesian inference. Bouncy particle sampler (BPS) is a method that performs sampling using uniform linear motion and elastic collisions. Since BPS does not require time discretization, it is expected to be more advantageous than the widely used Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) and Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC) for distributions with large curvature changes. To sample more efficiently from multimodal distributions, we propose BPS with parallel tempering (BPS-PT) in the infinite exchange limit, based on LMC-PT with the infinite exchange rate proposed in a previous study. Using a distribution with large curvature changes, BPS-PT showed estimation accuracy comparable to HMC-PT and LMC-PT, and achieved higher ESS per computational time. Therefore, BPS-PT is considered to be effective for distributions with large curvature changes.

papers.title: JaGNet: Detection, Identification and Position Error Correction of GNSS Jamming with Deep Temporal Graphs
papers.summary: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) underpin location-dependent mobile computing, such as railway signaling, public transport and fleet tracking, yet face growing disruption from low-cost jammers. Under moderate jamming, low-cost receivers keep reporting a valid fix, shifted by up to several meters and often without an interference flag. Their built-in defenses run in closed firmware, and existing data-driven position error correction methods are designed for multipath, require raw pseudoranges or operate on single epochs. We propose JaGNet, a single-layer heterogeneous graph convolutional LSTM over star graphs of the receiver and its satellites, which, from the standard receiver output alone, detects the jamming, identifies its type and power, and corrects the reported position only when jamming is detected. We evaluate it on new hardware-in-the-loop recordings of a commercial multi-constellation receiver under three jammer types at six powers, at six static locations and on eleven railway and bus routes. JaGNet detects 99.8 to 99.9% of the jammed 10-s windows with at most 1.0% false positives, against 64.7 to 66.2% for the receiver's own monitor, and identifies the jammer type in 95.2 to 96.6% of them. Trained in the laboratory only, it detects 97.7% of the Jammertest 2024 field windows with a C/N0 drop of 10 dB or more. It reduces the mean absolute position error by 67.5% at held-out locations and by 64.0% on held-out route repetitions, where its error is 20.2 cm below that of the strongest baseline, whereas at the static locations the attention-based baselines are within 0.4 cm of it.

papers.title: Bayesian Optimization under Uncertainty for Training a Scale Parameter in Stochastic Models
papers.summary: Hyperparameter tuning is a challenging problem especially when the system itself involves uncertainty. Due to noisy function evaluations, optimization under uncertainty can be computationally expensive. In this paper, we present a novel Bayesian optimization framework tailored for hyperparameter tuning under uncertainty, with a focus on optimizing a scale- or precision-type parameter in stochastic models. The proposed method employs a statistical surrogate for the underlying random variable, enabling analytical evaluation of the expectation operator. Moreover, we derive a closed-form expression for the optimizer of the random acquisition function, which significantly reduces computational cost per iteration. Numerical experiments demonstrate substantial gains in optimization efficiency: about 40-fold reduction in data usage relative to a Monte Carlo-based one-dimensional optimization scheme, and an order of magnitude improvement relative to a Gaussian process-based Bayesian optimization baseline.

papers.title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation through Latent Subspace Coefficients Search
papers.summary: Real-world deployment often exposes vision models to distribution shifts, making test-time adaptation (TTA) important for reliable prediction. Existing TTA methods can be difficult to deploy on edge devices because they require backpropagation, activation storage, or test-time batches, which increase computation, memory, and state. We propose \textbf{ELaTTA} (\textit{Efficient Latent Test-Time Adaptation}), a forward-only, gradient-free framework for single-instance TTA. ELaTTA freezes the pretrained model and adapts each test input by searching a low-dimensional coefficient vector in a principal latent subspace computed offline from a source-domain cache. The basis is stored once and source data are discarded before deployment. At test time, CMA-ES performs covariance-adaptive Gaussian search, ranks candidate corrections by prediction entropy, and selects the best candidate within a fixed evaluation budget. On five visual benchmarks spanning corruption, natural, rendition, sketch, and cross-domain shifts, ELaTTA provides strong accuracy under strict and continual single-instance protocols. In the strict single-instance comparison, MEMO requires \emph{64.7$\times$} the computation and \emph{12.4$\times$} the peak memory of ELaTTA. A complementary keyword-spotting experiment shows that the same coefficient-search design transfers beyond vision. We further demonstrate ViT-Base adaptation on a Raspberry Pi 5, confirming the feasibility of deploying ELaTTA on an edge device.

papers.title: Stochastic Difference-of-Convex Optimization with Momentum
papers.summary: We study the online stochastic difference-of-convex (DC) program $\min_{x \in R^n} F(x) = G(x) - H(x) + r_1(x) - r_2(x)$, which covers sparse learning with nonconvex penalties, robust regression with smooth robust losses, and non-negative positive--unlabeled learning. We propose \emph{momentum-based DCA} (MDCA), which combines a damped DCA step with a momentum estimator for $\nabla H$ and uses a constant per-iteration batch size. With exact solutions of the convex subproblems, MDCA with Polyak momentum uses $\mathcal{O}( \epsilon^{-4})$ stochastic gradients of $H$ to reach $\epsilon$-stationarity, and momentum-based variance reduction (MVR) uses $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$ under averaged smoothness, with a single $\mathcal O(\epsilon^{-1})$ warm-up batch in place of the periodic large batches of DCA-PAGE, whose $\epsilon$-dependence it matches. We also introduce a single-loop variant (S-MDCA) that replaces the subproblem solve by one stochastic prox-gradient step; for every fixed smoothing parameter $\gamma$ for which the separately smoothed surrogate $F_\gamma$ is bounded below, it reaches $\epsilon$-stationarity of $F_\gamma$ in $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ iterations, which does not by itself imply stationarity of $F$. A variance--drift trade-off lemma describes how the momentum parameter trades estimator variance against iterate-drift bias in steady-state upper bounds. Guarantees are given for two criteria: the critical-distance measure, and a DCA fixed-point residual that requires no smoothness of $r_2$ and vanishes exactly at DC-critical points; both give the same $\epsilon$-dependence. Experiments on two LIBSVM classification datasets illustrate the methods' behaviour.

papers.title: Deep Jump Gaussian Processes for Surrogate Modeling of High-Dimensional Piecewise Continuous Functions
papers.summary: We introduce Deep Jump Gaussian Processes (DJGP), a novel method for surrogate modeling of a piecewise continuous function on a high-dimensional domain. DJGP addresses the limitations of conventional Jump Gaussian Processes (JGP) in high-dimensional input spaces by integrating region-specific, locally linear projections with JGP modeling. These projections employ region-dependent matrices to capture local low-dimensional subspace structures, making them well suited to the inherently localized modeling behavior of JGPs, a variant of local Gaussian processes. To control model complexity, we place a Gaussian Process prior on the projection matrices, allowing them to evolve smoothly across the input space. The projected inputs are then modeled with a JGP to capture piecewise continuous relationships with the response. This yields a distinctive two-layer deep learning of GP/JGP. We further develop a scalable variational inference algorithm to jointly learn the projection matrices and JGP hyperparameters. Rigorous theoretical analysis and extensive empirical studies are provided to justify the proposed approach. In particular, we derive an oracle error bound for DJGP and decompose it into four distinct sources of error, which are then linked to practical implications. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets demonstrate that DJGP achieves superior predictive accuracy and more reliable uncertainty quantification compared with existing methods.

papers.title: Reviving Stale Updates: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Asynchronous Federated Learning
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw data, yet its scalability is limited by synchronization overhead. Asynchronous federated learning (AFL) alleviates this issue by allowing clients to communicate independently, thereby improving wall-clock efficiency in large-scale, hardware-heterogeneous environments. However, asynchrony introduces updates computed on outdated global models (staleness) that can destabilize optimization and hinder convergence. We propose FedRevive, an AFL framework that revives stale updates through data-free knowledge distillation (DFKD). FedRevive integrates parameter-space aggregation with a server-side DFKD process that transfers knowledge from stale client updates to the current global model without access to data. A meta-learned generator synthesizes pseudo-samples for multi-teacher distillation. A hybrid aggregation scheme combining raw with DFKD updates effectively mitigates staleness while retaining AFL scalability. Experiments on vision and text benchmarks show that FedRevive achieves faster training by up to 29.7% and higher final accuracy by up to 11.4 percentage points than baselines.

papers.title: The Optimization Landscape of Carath\'eodory Decomposition of Toeplitz Covariances
papers.summary: Toeplitz covariance estimation is a classical signal processing problem, yet the geometry of the Gaussian maximum-likelihood objective remains only partially understood. Recent Newton-type, majorization-minimization, and gradient-based methods often solve the nonconvex problem globally with enough samples, but also reveal a difficult computational landscape. We study this phenomenon through an overparameterized Carath\'eodory representation, which parameterizes the covariance by the frequencies and amplitudes of steering vectors. A simple example shows that, for any uniform frequency grid, optimizing only the amplitudes can leave a positive error even in the population setting, which motivates optimizing the frequencies as well. Our main result proves that this nonlinear parameterization adds no stationary points: for any sample covariance, every stationary point with a positive definite covariance gives a stationary point of the Toeplitz maximum-likelihood problem. In the population setting, every such point therefore recovers the true covariance. We also prove that gradient descent converges to the true covariance in the population setting, and to the unique maximum likelihood estimate when the sample covariance is close enough to the true covariance. These results do not require overparameterization. Numerically, overparameterization speeds up gradient descent and gives a more accurate estimate for a fixed number of iterations.

papers.title: A Nesterov-Accelerated Byzantine-Robust Federated Learning
papers.summary: We investigate robust federated learning, where a group of workers collaboratively train a shared model under the orchestration of a central server in the presence of Byzantine adversaries capable of arbitrary and potentially malicious behaviors. To simultaneously enhance communication efficiency and resilience against such adversaries, we propose a Byzantine-resilient Nesterov-accelerated federated learning (Byrd-NAFL) algorithm. Byrd-NAFL seamlessly integrates Nesterov's momentum into the federated learning process alongside Byzantine-resilient aggregation rules to achieve fast and safe convergence against gradient corruption. We establish a finite-time convergence guarantee for Byrd-NAFL under non-convex and smooth loss functions with relaxed assumptions on the aggregated gradients. Extensive numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of Byrd-NAFL and demonstrate the superiority over existing benchmarks in terms of convergence speed, accuracy, and resilience to diverse malicious attacks.

papers.title: QuAnTS: Question Answering on Time Series
papers.summary: Text offers intuitive access to information. This can, in particular, complement the density of numerical time series, thereby enabling improved interactions with time series models to enhance accessibility and decision-making. While the creation of question-answering datasets and models has recently seen remarkable growth, most research focuses on question answering (QA) on vision and text, with time series receiving minute attention. To bridge this gap, we propose a challenging novel time series QA (TSQA) dataset, QuAnTS, for Question Answering on Time Series data. Specifically, we pose a wide variety of questions and answers about human motion in the form of tracked skeleton trajectories. We verify that the large-scale QuAnTS dataset is well-formed and comprehensive through extensive experiments. Thoroughly evaluating existing and newly proposed baselines then lays the groundwork for a deeper exploration of TSQA using QuAnTS. Additionally, we provide human performances as a key reference for gauging the practical usability of such models. We hope to encourage future research on interacting with time series models through text, enabling better decision-making and more transparent systems.

papers.title: From Topology to Retrieval: Decoding Embedding Spaces with Unified Signatures
papers.summary: Studying the shape of text embedding spaces enhances our understanding of model behavior and how geometry affects downstream task performance. While a range of topological and geometric metrics have been explored, they are typically analyzed in isolation, and the connections between them remain largely unknown. In this paper, we present Unified Topological Signatures (UTS) for characterizing the structure of embedding spaces. We evaluate our method across a wide range of text embedding models and retrieval datasets, finding that it outperforms individual metrics in downstream performance prediction. Through several experiments, we demonstrate that the signatures characterize embedding spaces more accurately, improve the prediction of model-specific properties and biases, and reveal novel insights into representational similarity that challenge the global claims of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

papers.title: PISA: Prioritized Invariant Subgraph Aggregation for Out-of-Distribution Generalization on Graphs
papers.summary: Invariant learning on graphs aims to build predictors that rely on causal substructures rather than on environment-specific shortcuts. Current methods extract either a single invariant subgraph (CIGA) or, more recently, a set of diverse invariant subgraphs (SuGAr). We observe that the second half of the multi-subgraph pipeline, "how the extracted subgraphs are combined" has gone essentially unexamined; existing methods average branch predictions uniformly or select one greedily. We show that this is precisely where accuracy is lost. A minimum-variance combination argument establishes that uniform averaging is optimal only when every branch carries the same total error covariance with the ensemble---a knife edge balance that second order exchangeability guarantees and that the diversity regularizer used to obtain multiple subgraphs is explicitly designed to break. We then show that invariance is closed under post composition; because the branches are frozen and read the graph only through their invariant subgraphs, any measurable aggregator of their outputs remains invariant, and the aggregate's environment gap is bounded by the branches' residual invariance violation uniformly over aggregators. Learning the combination rule by plain empirical risk minimization is therefore safe, and aggregator capacity trades off against estimation error rather than robustness. PISA instantiates this with a lightweight instance-conditional MLP over stacked branch logits, trained on frozen branches at negligible cost. Across 15 synthetic and real benchmarks, PISA improves the average over the strongest prior method by 2.96 points on synthetic shifts and 1.74 points on realistic shifts, with per-dataset gains up to 5.90 points, and nearly doubles SuGAr's improvement over ERM on the six DrugOOD tasks (from +2.76 to +5.07 ROC-AUC).

papers.title: UMM-RM: An Upcycle-and-Merge MoE Reward Model for Mitigating Reward Hacking
papers.summary: Reward models (RMs) are critical to reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). However, policy models can exploit biases or spurious correlations in dense RMs, causing reward hacking: RM scores rise while alignment with human preferences deteriorates, especially under distribution shift. We propose UMM-RM (Upcycle-and-Merge MoE Reward Model), which copies the feed-forward layers of an SFT checkpoint to initialize shared and routed experts, then trains the model on preference data. The always-active shared expert captures instruction-agnostic preference signals, while routed experts model fine-grained preferences across instructions or tasks. The experts are then merged into a single dense RM using learnable weights, preserving the robustness and exploitation resistance of expert diversity without MoE or ensemble inference overhead. Across multiple base models and preference datasets, UMM-RM improves preference accuracy, reduces reward hacking during PPO training, and achieves more stable preference alignment than standard dense RMs.

papers.title: Understanding Negative Learning in Large Language Model Fine-tuning
papers.summary: Negative learning has never been more important than it is today, particularly in large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, where it underpins machine unlearning, preference- and reward-based optimization, and exploratory data generation. Yet its functional role remains a subject of ongoing debate, with existing work variously characterizing it as forgetting, regularization, or target shaping. However, analytical support focuses primarily on the single-update scale, while empirical results at the trajectory scale are typically obtained under negative-only training and may not extend to composite objectives in which it interacts with other components. To develop a deeper understanding, we introduce a gradient-based endpoint probing framework that can examine negative updates separately throughout training. Our analysis reveals that negative learning plays different roles across algorithms and training phases. For example, in off-policy DPO, it acts more like a regularizer early in training and shows evidence of target shaping only toward out-of-distribution endpoints and only in later phases. In on-policy PPO and GRPO, by contrast, negative updates offset endpoint-aligned positive learning without stable target shaping, consistent with a role in sustaining exploration. Guided by these findings, we develop a family of stage-aware methods that modulate the strength of negative updates throughout training, improving fine-tuning performance across tasks.

papers.title: Quantum-Classical Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving Reservoir Seepage Equations
papers.summary: Solving reservoir seepage partial differential equations (PDEs) is critical for hydrocarbon development optimization and production forecasting. Conventional numerical solvers suffer from mesh errors and high computational cost. Standard Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are limited by inefficient parameters. They also face weak high-dimensional representation and poor nonlinear fitting ability. We adapt the Discrete Variable (DV)-Circuit Quantum-Classical Physics-Informed Neural Network (QCPINN) to tackle these drawbacks. This work applies the method to four representative reservoir seepage models. The models cover heterogeneous single-phase pressure diffusion. They also include nonlinear Buckley-Leverett two-phase waterflooding. Another case is adsorption-coupled convection-diffusion compositional flow. The last one refers to fully coupled pressure-saturation two-phase flow with exponential permeability heterogeneity. The QCPINN combines classical preprocessing and postprocessing networks with a DV quantum core. It leverages quantum entanglement and superposition to boost high-dimensional feature mapping. Physical constraints are embedded within the framework to guarantee physically consistent solutions. We evaluate three quantum circuit topologies including Cascade, Cross-mesh and Alternate. Numerical tests prove QCPINNs outperform classical PINNs in prediction accuracy, and the circuit topologies show case-specific performance with clear applicable ranges. This work verifies QCPINN's practicability for reservoir engineering. It bridges quantum computing research with oilfield industrial applications.

papers.title: ASCIIBench: Evaluating Language-Model-Based Understanding of Visually-Oriented Text
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated several emergent behaviors with scale, including reasoning and fluency in long-form text generation. However, they continue to struggle with tasks requiring precise spatial and positional reasoning. ASCII art, a symbolic medium where characters encode structure and form, provides a unique probe of this limitation. We introduce ASCIIBench, a novel benchmark for evaluating both the generation and classification of ASCII-text images. ASCIIBench consists of a filtered dataset of 5,135 class-labeled ASCII images and is, to our knowledge, the first publicly available benchmark of its kind. Alongside the dataset, we release weights for a fine-tuned CLIP model adapted to capture ASCII structure, enabling the evaluation of LLM-generated ASCII art. Our analysis shows that cosine similarity over CLIP embeddings fails to separate most ASCII categories, yielding chance-level performance even for low-variance classes. In contrast, classes with high internal mean similarity exhibit clear discriminability, revealing that the bottleneck lies in representation rather than generational variance. These findings position ASCII art as a stress test for multimodal representations and motivate the development of new embedding methods or evaluation metrics tailored to symbolic visual modalities. All resources are available at https://github.com/ASCIIBench/ASCIIBench.

papers.title: Wait, Wait, Wait... Why Do Reasoning Models Loop?
papers.summary: Reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1) generate long chains of thought to solve harder problems, but they often loop, repeating the same text at low temperatures or with greedy decoding. We study why this happens and what role temperature plays. With open reasoning models, we find that looping is common at low temperature. Larger models tend to loop less, and distilled students loop significantly even when their teachers rarely do. This points to mismatches between the training distribution and the learned model, which we refer to as errors in learning, as a key cause. To understand how such errors cause loops, we introduce a synthetic graph reasoning task and demonstrate two mechanisms. First, risk aversion caused by hardness of learning: when the correct progress-making action is hard to learn but an easy cyclic action is available, the model puts relatively more probability on the cyclic action and gets stuck. Second, even when there is no hardness, Transformers show an inductive bias toward temporally correlated errors, so the same few actions keep being chosen and loops appear. Higher temperature reduces looping by promoting exploration, but it does not fix the errors in learning, so generations remain much longer than necessary at high temperature; in this sense, temperature is a stopgap rather than a holistic solution. We end with a discussion of training-time interventions aimed at directly reducing errors in learning.

papers.title: Deep Learning and Elicitability for McKean-Vlasov FBSDEs With Common Noise
papers.summary: We present a novel numerical method for solving McKean-Vlasov forward-backward stochastic differential equations (MV--FBSDEs) with common noise, combining Picard iterations, elicitability and deep learning. The key innovation involves elicitability to derive a path-wise loss function, enabling efficient training of neural networks to approximate both the backward process and the conditional expectations arising from common noise -- without requiring computationally expensive nested Monte Carlo simulations. The mean-field interaction term is parameterized via a recurrent neural network trained to minimize an elicitable score, while the backward process is approximated through a hybrid feedforward and recurrent network representing the decoupling field. We validate the algorithm on a systemic risk inter-bank borrowing and lending model, where analytical solutions exist, demonstrating accurate recovery of the true solution. We further extend the model to quantile--mediated interactions, showcasing the flexibility of the elicitability framework beyond conditional means or moments. Finally, we apply the method to a non-stationary Aiyagari-Bewley-Huggett economic growth model with endogenous interest rates, illustrating its applicability to complex mean-field games without closed-form solutions.

papers.title: AdvJudge-Zero: Binary Decision Flips in LLM-as-a-Judge via Adversarial Control Tokens
papers.summary: LLM-as-a-Judge systems supply the reward signal in modern RLHF and RLVR pipelines, but their binary verdict reduces to a single linear readout F_gap on one hidden state. We show this readout is shallow enough that short, low-perplexity tokens flip the verdict from "No" to "Yes". These tokens are sampled from the judge's own next-token distribution at the response position, with no manual seed set and no gradient-based optimization. Our procedure, AdvJudge-Zero, reaches $>$90% ensemble false-positive rate on 22 of 24 (model, dataset) cells across six Qwen, Llama, and Gemma judges, versus 54-72% for the prior curated 10-token benchmark, and the discovered surface transfers cross-format to a 70B scalar reward model. The same discovered pool enables a defense: a LoRA fine-tune stratified by a 9-class mechanism taxonomy hardens cross-family generalization where naive sampling on the same pool fails, with mechanism breadth rather than pool size carrying the gain. Under GRPO training, the hardened judge eliminates the reward-collapse failures (false-positive spikes and length collapse) we observe in the unhardened baseline on both MATH and GSM8K at ten seeds per condition. The discovered pool, the mechanism taxonomy, and per-prompt flip records will be released under responsible disclosure.

papers.title: KerJEPA: Kernel Discrepancies for Euclidean Self-Supervised Learning
papers.summary: Breakthroughs in self-supervised Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have established that regularizing Euclidean representations toward isotropic Gaussian priors yields provable gains in training stability and downstream generalization. We introduce a new, flexible family of Euclidean joint embedding self-supervised learning algorithms with kernel-based regularizers. One instance of this family corresponds to the SIGReg Epps-Pulley regularizer which approximates a sliced Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) with a Gaussian prior and Gaussian kernel. By expanding the class of viable kernels and priors and computing the closed-form high-dimensional limit of sliced discrepancies, we develop alternative methods with improved training stability and design flexibility and leverage those techniques to train strong vision learners at scale.

papers.title: Unrolled Neural Networks for Constrained Optimization
papers.summary: We develop unrolled neural networks to solve constrained optimization problems, offering accelerated, learnable counterparts to dual ascent (DA) algorithms. Our framework, termed constrained dual unrolling (CDU), comprises two coupled neural networks that jointly approximate the saddle point of the Lagrangian. The primal network emulates an iterative optimizer that finds a stationary point of the Lagrangian for a given dual multiplier, sampled from an unknown distribution. The dual network generates trajectories towards the optimal multipliers across its layers while querying the primal network at each layer. Unlike standard unrolling, which maps the updates of a prescribed iterative solver directly to network layers, CDU preserves the underlying optimization dynamics while learning the update mappings. The desired primal-dual dynamics are therefore induced through constrained learning by enforcing primal-descent and dual-ascent constraints. We formulate training the two networks as a nested optimization problem and propose an alternating procedure that updates the primal and dual networks in turn, mitigating uncertainty in the multiplier distribution required for primal network training. We establish theoretical guarantees on the feasibility and optimality of the coupled networks. We numerically evaluate the framework on quadratic programs (QPs) with linear constraints and power allocation in wireless networks.

papers.title: Signal from Structure: Exploiting Submodular Upper Bounds in Generative Flow Networks
papers.summary: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets; GFNs) are a class of generative models that learn to sample compositional objects proportional to their a priori unknown value, their reward. We focus on the case where the reward has a specified, actionable structure, namely that it is submodular. We show submodularity can be harnessed to retrieve upper bounds on the reward of compositional objects that have not yet been observed. We provide in-depth analyses of the probability of such bounds occurring, as well as how many unobserved compositional objects can be covered by a bound. Following the Optimism in the Face of Uncertainty principle, we then introduce SUBo-GFN , which uses the submodular upper bounds to train a GFN. We show that SUBo-GFN generates orders of magnitude more learning signal than classical GFNs for the same number of queries to the reward function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SUBo-GFN in terms of distribution matching and high-quality candidate generation on graph submodular tasks.

papers.title: Mechanistic Evidence for Spectral Structures in Prior-Data Fitted Networks
papers.summary: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) perform approximate Bayesian inference in a single forward pass, and tabular foundation models (TFMs) built on them are now widely used. To understand what networks infer internally, recent mechanistic studies of TFMs locate where predictions form, but treat these models as tabular predictors rather than as PFNs. It therefore remains unknown whether PFNs represent the spectral content of their context, the quantity that specifies a stationary kernel, and whether this content can be read out as an explicit kernel. We answer both questions. First, across seven PFNs, including four pretrained TFMs and a model trained only on a decision-tree prior, a linear probe on the residual stream recovers the frequency of the context with $R^2 \geq 0.95$. This structure is led by a single principal direction. Second, activation and subspace patching show that the network uses the structure through a low-dimensional subspace, where a few spectral directions move predictions far more than random ones. This holds even for the decision-tree model, so a spectral training prior is not required. On real datasets with up to 499 features, 64 of the 192 directions of TabPFN, chosen without labels, carry 85 to 95\% of the causal effect of the context in all but one pair. Third, we introduce a Filter Bank Decoder that turns frozen PFN representations into an explicit stationary kernel through Bochner's theorem. Without any test-time optimization, the decoded kernel supports Gaussian process regression competitive with deep kernel learning and random Fourier features at about $200\times$ lower cost. PFN latents therefore hold spectral structure that is causally used and recoverable as a portable kernel.

papers.title: Transfer Denoising of Low-Rank Plus Sparse Matrices under Ambient and Rank Growth
papers.summary: We study transfer learning for low-rank plus sparse matrix denoising when both ambient and latent dimensions grow. A data-rich source task provides subspace information for a higher-dimensional, data-scarce target with a small rank increment and localized sparse edits. We develop an anchored alternating-projection estimator that preserves transferred subspaces while learning target-specific coefficients, additional latent directions, and sparse modifications. We establish deterministic error bounds that separate target noise, representation growth, and source-estimation error, identifying improved rates through small structural increments and reduced noise within inherited subspaces. We further extend it to approximate anchoring quantifies robustness to subspace mismatch. We establish application-specific guarantees for Markov transition matrix estimation from single trajectories with dependent noise and for structured covariance estimation, with the latter analysis provided in the appendix. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over non-transfer baselines on synthetic data and an approximately 45\% reduction in principal-angle error on a NYC taxi transition-estimation task with expanding state spaces.

papers.title: Federate the Router: Learning Language Model Routers with Sparse and Decentralized Evaluations
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly accessed as remotely hosted services by edge and enterprise clients that cannot run frontier models locally. Since models vary widely in capability and price, routing queries to models that balance quality and inference cost is essential. Existing router approaches assume access to centralized query-model evaluation data. However, these data are often fragmented across clients, such as end users and organizations, and are privacy-sensitive, which makes centralizing data infeasible. Additionally, per-client router training is ineffective since local evaluation data is limited and covers only a restricted query distribution and a biased subset of model evaluations. We introduce the first federated framework for LLM routing, enabling clients to learn a shared routing policy from local offline query-model evaluation data. Our framework supports both parametric multilayer perceptron router and nonparametric K-means router under heterogeneous client query distributions and non-uniform model coverage. Across three benchmarks, federated collaboration improves the accuracy-cost frontier over client-local routers, both via increased effective model coverage and better query generalization. Our theoretical results also validate that federated training reduces routing suboptimality.
