papers.title: Comparative Robustness of Mach-Zehender and Microring Photonic Matrix Multipliers Under Laser RIN and Thermal Drift
papers.summary: Photonic matrix multipliers can accelerate neural-network inference, but their practical utility depends on how optical weight elements respond to source noise, thermal variation, and calibration error. This paper compares Mach-Zehnder modulator (MZM) and microring-resonator (MRR) implementations under laser relative-intensity noise (RIN), column-wise thermal/phase drift, and their joint action. Two CIFAR-10 classifiers - a compact four-layer CNN and ResNet-8 - are mapped to matched photonic multiply-accumulate chains using common source-distribution, detection, numerical, and calibration assumptions. Both architectures reproduce the same zero-perturbation baseline for each workload: 79.5% classification accuracy for the Small CNN and 70.0% for ResNet-8. Robustness is then evaluated using separate RIN-only and drift-only sweeps and a full two-dimensional RIN-drift grid, with dimensionless RMS perturbation levels extending from 0.5% to 20%. The analysis reports classification accuracy, class normalized confusion matrices, rolling-accuracy traces, one-dimensional robustness curves, and multidimensional response surfaces. Device equations and parameter definitions follow the models implemented in the QPI Labs Photonic Inference Simulator, with shared laser fluctuations propagated as correlated multiplicative noise and slow drift represented as a per-output-column perturbation of calibrated weights. All numerical results are generated from recorded experiment configurations and random seeds. The study provides a controlled system-level framework for comparing interferometric and resonant photonic weight elements while limiting conclusions to the implemented device models, perturbation ranges, calibration policy, and neural-network workloads.

papers.title: Local sensing of gas microflows using a levitated nanoparticle
papers.summary: Local measurements of gas flow in microscale geometries remain challenging due to the difficulty of micromechanical sensors implantation. Here, we use a levitated nanoparticle as a minimally invasive probe to map, with high spatial resolution, both the local pressure and velocity gas flow for a canonical example - a micropipe subjected to a pressure gradient. This technique enables characterization of nonequilibrium gas transport across several flow regimes, from slip flow to free-molecular flow. We directly observe the emergence of a nonlinear pressure distribution at large pressure ratios and obtain agreement with kinetic-theory predictions and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo calculations. These results introduce levitated nanoparticles as powerful and reconfigurable probes for microchannel gas sensing, with applications in microtechnology, micro-chemistry, and bioengineering.

papers.title: From Microresonator to Packaged Microcomb System: Fiber-Coupled Module and System Integration
papers.summary: We demonstrate a compact and robust soliton microcomb source designed for field-deployable operation. A directly fiber-coupled SiN microresonator was integrated with precise thermal control into a palm-sized module, reducing the footprint and volume by 16- and 81-fold, respectively. The module, together with the laser sources and optical amplifiers required for microcomb generation, was further integrated into a 19-inch rack-mounted enclosure, achieving system-level footprint and volume reductions of 2.3- and 3.7-fold, respectively. The packaged system achieved a 90% manual startup success rate and maintained continuous soliton operation for 18.8 days, while remaining operational under substantial temperature variations. A state-based automated startup scheme using discrete microcomb-state evaluation achieved single-soliton generation without manual intervention with success rates of 50% within 2 min and 60% within 3 min. Moreover, automated soliton initiation and sustained operation were demonstrated while the packaged microresonator module was directly subjected to random mechanical vibration. These results provide a practical platform for compact, robust, and field-deployable microcomb sources.

papers.title: BOLD PSF: Impact of k-space trajectories and timing on the depiction of T2* contrast
papers.summary: The timing of BOLD-fMRI is typically chosen such that TE matches T2*. This assumes contrast being exclusively elicited by signal differences at TE. While sensible for short or TE-symmetric readouts, such as EPIs, it oversimplifies contrast generation for longer or TE-asymmetric trajectories, such as spirals. We propose the concept of a BOLD PSF for a more comprehensive perspective on the imaging characteristics of a functional experiment. Our findings indicate that TE can be reduced for spiral-out without sacrificing BOLD-sensitivity when compared to EPI. Furthermore, we characterize the intrinsic trade-off between specificity and resolution of the BOLD response under varying TE.

papers.title: Identification of effective transport physics and optimal feedback control: Experimental demonstration on a 1600-fan wind generator
papers.summary: Distributed-input distributed-output (DIDO) systems arise in numerous engineering applications where large numbers of actuators generate spatially distributed physical fields that are monitored by distributed sensors. Developing physically interpretable models that enable real-time optimal control of these systems remains challenging because of the high dimensionality and strong spatial coupling between inputs and outputs. In this work, we propose a physics-based framework for modeling and closed-loop optimal control of DIDO systems from experimental input-output data. First, an effective partial differential equation (PDE) is selected among candidate transport models and discretized on the actuator grid to obtain a minimum-grid representation. Second, the PDE is solved in closed form, which yields an input-output operator with only four physically interpretable parameters. Third, the operator is incorporated into an iterative, constrained quadratic program that accounts for the actuator limits. The framework is demonstrated on the inner 40 x 40 section of the world's highest-resolution Fan Array Wind Generator (FAWG), comprising 1600 independently controlled fans with 36 distributed velocity measurements. The model describes the spatial interaction between the 1600 actuators and the measured velocity field with normalized mean absolute prediction errors of 11-20% for representative actuation patterns. The closed-loop controller reproduces all three prescribed two-dimensional velocity fields with a normalized mean absolute error below 2.3% in fewer than 10 iterations.

papers.title: A reduced model for neoclassical transport in non-axisymmetric magnetic configurations
papers.summary: A unified framework is proposed to compute a neoclassical equilibrium for tokamaks with non-axisymmetric magnetic perturbations, based on a Hamiltonian description combined with a variational approach that relies on a principle of minimum entropy production. This approach allows for a transparent identification of the respective contributions from different classes of trapped particles in magnetic well minima. Analytic expressions are derived for specific collisionality regimes, and a fast and efficient numerical procedure is devised to compute the entropy production rate. Finding the extremum of the entropy production leads to tractable expressions of transport coefficients that can be computed quickly and efficiently.

papers.title: Tersoff-NN: Hybrid Machine-Learned Bond-Order Extension of the Tersoff Potential
papers.summary: Accurate, robust, and efficient interatomic potentials are highly desirable for large-scale molecular dynamics simulations. Although machine-learning interatomic potentials can reproduce first-principles potential-energy surfaces with high accuracy, they typically incur higher computational costs than conventional empirical potentials and may be less reliable outside their training domains. We developed Tersoff-NN, a hybrid machine-learning potential for Si, which retains the analytical radial interactions and cutoff structure of the Tersoff potential while representing its environment-dependent bond-order factor using compact neural networks (NNs). Benchmarks for 32,768-atom systems show that Tersoff-NN is 4-12 times faster than the Behler-Parrinello-type NN potentials tested in this study. Tersoff-NN improves the short-range structure of liquid Si relative to the conventional Tersoff potential, closely reproduces the ab initio radial and angular distributions, and reproduces the equilibrium structure of diamond Si and qualitative energetic trends among several crystalline phases. Furthermore, melt-quench simulations reveal a disordered solid with predominantly four-coordinated, tetrahedral-like local environments. Additionally, characteristic reconstruction motifs are retained on Si surfaces despite their exclusion from the training dataset. A direct comparison with an alternative atom-centered bond-order NN highlights the critical role of physical constraints in ensuring dynamic stability. Despite exhibiting comparable validation errors, the selected triplet-based architecture remains stable, while an alternative model exhibits unphysical bond-order growth and atomic collapse. These results confirm that learning only the bond-order term improves the description of diverse Si environments while retaining substantial computational efficiency and enhancing dynamical stability.

papers.title: Tornado Wave-Encoded Point Spread Functions for Multi-Period Three-Dimensional Localization Imaging
papers.summary: Three-dimensional (3D) localization microscopy using rotational point spread functions (PSFs) is fundamentally challenged by limited axial range, poor PSF compactness, and depth-decoding ambiguity -- particularly in dense specimens with heavy PSF overlap. To address these limitations, we introduce a 3D localization approach based on tornado wave (ToW)-PSFs, combined with a convolutional neural network (CNN) designed to decode continuous rotational patterns and resolve multi-period axial ambiguity. Our engineered PSF encodes the 3D position of each nanoparticle into a compact double-lobe pattern whose orientation rotates with axial position. This design yields a clean, well-defined structural evolution across an unprecedented 15 um axial range, with an average rotation rate of 21.8 degrees/um, ensuring robust long-range depth encoding. To recover coordinates from overlapping emitters, we systematically benchmark a conventional matching-pursuit (MP) algorithm against our CNN. While MP performs adequately in sparse scenes, the CNN demonstrates exceptional robustness in dense fields, achieving a 70.24% localization accuracy at 20 particles per image-substantially outperforming MP's 22.52% -- while also significantly suppressing axial period-jump errors. Experimental validation on nanoparticles confirms reliable single- and multi-particle localization throughout the entire working range. Our results establish ToW-PSFs as a powerful and practical optical encoding strategy for high-density, extended-range 3D localization imaging.

papers.title: Proposal for a multi-ion optical clock with hundreds of ions
papers.summary: Scaling trapped-ion optical clocks to hundreds of ions remains a major challenge due to inhomogeneous frequency shifts in large ion crystals. Here, we propose a circular surface-trap architecture for a multi-ion optical clock with hundreds of ions. The rotational symmetry of the ion crystal suppresses the main sources of inhomogeneity, quadrupole shift.We investigate the feasibility of a clock based on a ring crystal of 400 $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^{+}$ ions and propose a suitable experimental setup configuration. We have shown that circular configuration of ions leads to suppression by two orders of magnitude of the quadrupole shift comparing to the linear trap. Combined with stray-field compensation and dynamical decoupling techniques, this architecture provides a pathway toward multi-ion optical clocks with fractional frequency uncertainty at the $10^{-18}$ level and an expected 20-fold improvement in frequency stability compared to single ion clocks.

papers.title: Brilliance: toward autonomous computational research in particle accelerator physics
papers.summary: Computational research in physics requires continuous interplay between simulation and scientific interpretation, demanding substantial specialist effort. Here we introduce Brilliance, a research agent that combines large language models, reusable physics knowledge and numerical simulation to conduct adaptive investigations in accelerator physics. Given a single user prompt, Brilliance designs a fourth-generation synchrotron light source that meets coupled emittance and nonlinear-acceptance requirements. Further exploration yields a design combining sub-10-pm emittance with a large dynamic aperture under realistic engineering constraints, suggesting a route towards hard-X-ray diffraction-limited operation, although the momentum-acceptance target remains unmet. Brilliance also calibrates a model of an operating light source against measured responses, accurately inferring its lattice and calibration errors. Across these studies, Brilliance autonomously revises its computational strategies in response to numerical evidence. These results demonstrate a route towards delegating sustained scientific investigations to agents equipped with domain expertise and numerical tools.

papers.title: Intrinsic Orbital Nernst Effect in Real Photonic Bands
papers.summary: We predict an intrinsic orbital Nernst effect in reciprocal photonic lattices with real Bloch modes. In the collisionless regime, a thermal gradient generates a transverse angular-displacement response although band angular moments and ordinary Berry curvatures vanish. The response is carried by angular-density dipoles formed through virtual mixing of distinct spatial modes. Their correlation with band velocity survives thermal averaging and is independently recovered from the angular-density readout of unitarily evolved wave packets. Two controls expose the mechanism: a fixed-generator two-level system has zero antisymmetric intrinsic response, and flattening the dispersion suppresses transport without changing the eigenstates. A canonical scalar Maxwell calculation realizes the effect through symmetry-selected virtual channels, even when one band dominates the thermal population. These findings establish an orbital-dipole mechanism for intrinsic thermal angular transport in real photonic bands.

papers.title: Broadband 600- and 1200-GHz Subharmonically Pumped Schottky Diode Mixers
papers.summary: A subharmonic mixer topology is introduced that uses quarter-wave stubs to create virtual RF/LO grounds and provide impedance matching in close proximity to the antiparallel Schottky barrier diode pair, thereby reducing the electrical length and enabling broadband operation. The 600-GHz mixer demonstrates approximately 20% RF bandwidth with a DSB receiver noise temperature below 1300 K across most of the measured band, while the 1200-GHz implementation achieves DSB receiver noise temperatures below 3000 K over a broad frequency range. Both mixers are characterized at room temperature with approximately 2 mW of LO power. The 600-GHz mixer is used in the Submillimeter Wave Instrument (SWI) onboard ESA's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer. Overall, these results demonstrate state-of-the-art room-temperature performance for broadband receiver front ends targeting atmospheric research and remote-sensing applications.

papers.title: Financial Interactions and Collective States: Part III. Description of Dynamic Collective States
papers.summary: In a series of papers, we analyzed the mechanisms of capital allocation and accumulation among firms, investors, and banks within the framework of Field Economics. At the macro level, we found that multiple collective states may emerge, each organized in groups of agents characterized by distinct levels of disposable capital, returns, and stakes across sectors. This multiplicity of collective states reflects the inherent instability and default-prone nature of financial markets. It also underscores the necessity of transitions among these states. These transitions were not fully accounted for in our previous description of collective states, where we only considered marginal fluctuations around equilibrium levels. To fill this gap, the present paper aims to characterize the possible dynamic mechanisms underlying transitions between these collective states. It reviews and extends our previous analysis by examining their probability and stability. By introducing the notion of dynamic sub-collective states, it explores potential patterns of transition-such as morphing, merging, or splitting-among collective states. This study thus provides the foundational tools and analytical framework that will be employed to develop a field-theoretic description of dynamic collective states.

papers.title: Kernel-Level Constant-Potential Molecular Dynamics in GROMACS
papers.summary: How charge rearranges within an electrode shapes the behavior of batteries, supercapacitors, and other electrochemical devices. Molecular simulations can capture this response by allowing the charge on each electrode atom to adjust to its surroundings, but repeatedly calculating these charges adds substantial computational cost. We present an open-source implementation of the constant-potential method in GROMACS that integrates these calculations into the program's optimized CPU and GPU routines. Comparisons with established codes validate the electrode charges, while charging, voltammetry, and impedance simulations demonstrate the response to changing electrical conditions. The implementation also supports electrodes that move or deform and models of finite metallic screening and electron spillover. In a pair of charged carbon nanotubes, allowing charge to move away from the facing surfaces reduces the repulsive force at contact by about half at an intermediate charge and keeps the pair bound where a uniform-charge model opens within the simulated time. These capabilities make the electrical response of electrodes accessible within GROMACS for studies of interfacial structure, charging dynamics, and electrode motion.

papers.title: Nonperturbative optomechanics with thin, weakly reflective intracavity dielectrics
papers.summary: Levitated dielectric sensors are often treated as perturbative probes of a pre-existing optical field. We show that this picture fails for a novel sensor geometry: a dielectric plate whose transverse extent captures the full optical mode. Even an optically thin sensor with modest refractive index can heavily restructure the intracavity fields, effectively partitioning a cavity into two subcavities with substantial cross-coupling and producing new optical resonances and trapping sites with properties which deviate from the standard intuition. Conventional perturbative expressions for the cavity frequency shift and optomechanical coupling depart from the exact solution at thicknesses as small as $\sim\lambda/(10n)$. Furthermore, cavity locking decreases the coupling and increases the trap stiffness by orders of magnitude, and the coupled subcavity structure permits appreciable optical cooling at zero detuning, a distinct behavior unique to this nonperturbative regime. These effects, sharing a common origin, establish a distinct regime of cavity optomechanics in which the sensor is no longer merely a probe of the cavity field, but an element that helps define it.

papers.title: Direct growth of crack-free stoichiometric silicon nitride on sapphire for wide-band photonics
papers.summary: Low-loss stoichiometric silicon nitride on oxidized silicon has emerged as the major wide-band photonics platform for nonlinear and quantum photonics. These films, deposited by low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD), are well known to have around 1000 MPa of residual tensile stress, which often leads to cracking when film thickness exceeds 400 nm. Although various stress-mitigation approaches can isolate or prevent cracking, this stress issue remains a major fabrication challenge. Low-residual-stress LPCVD stoichiometric silicon nitride on sapphire has also been reported and recently explored for photonics at telecommunication wavelengths. Here, we advance its development through systematic characterization, including thin-film stress analysis, ellipsometry and prism-coupling measurements of refractive index and loss, and swept-wavelength spectroscopy of fabricated photonic devices across a broad range of wavelengths. We demonstrate the direct growth of crack-free stoichiometric silicon nitride up to 2 {\mu}m thick with only 200 MPa of stress. Our fabricated devices show propagation losses of 0.35 dB/cm around 780 nm, 0.37 dB/cm around 1064 nm, and 0.25 dB/cm around 1630 nm. In addition, prism-coupling measurements indicate film losses below 1 dB/cm at wavelengths down to 500 nm. Our work highlights stoichiometric silicon nitride on sapphire as a promising wide-band photonics platform.

papers.title: Climate Sensitivity Derived from First-Principles Temperature Feedback Circuits
papers.summary: A long-standing challenge in climate science since the Charney Report in 1979 is to determine how much the Earth's climate warms in response to a unit external energy input at the top of the atmosphere (TOA). In this study, we show from first principles that temperature feedback within an atmosphere-surface column operates as a set of feedback circuits, each governed by an intrinsic gain less than unity, leading to geometric amplification of energy through successive feedback cycles. In particular, the surface-centered temperature feedback circuit determines the amplification of surface energy per unit TOA forcing. The surface energy amplification by non-temperature feedback is estimated from the amplification of solar energy absorption by downward longwave radiation at the surface in the climate mean state. Climate sensitivity then emerges as the product of these two amplifications scaled by the surface Planck feedback parameter. The climate sensitivity derived from the 1980-2000 climate mean state is 1.15 K (W m$^{-2}$)$^{-1}$. It yields a warming of 0.44 K from 1980-2000 to 2000-2020, consistent with the observed warming of 0.41 K, and equilibrium warmings of 3.02 and 5.83 K for CO$_2$ doubling and quadrupling, respectively, the former consistent with the Charney estimate near 3 degrees C. The framework provides a basis for predicting global surface temperature responses to other external forcing scenarios from the climate mean state.

papers.title: Nanofluid transport in Taylor bubble flows
papers.summary: Taylor bubble flows with nanoparticle suspensions are regularly encountered in non-isothermal chemical synthesis and microfluidics. Despite this, a complete mechanistic insight into the coupled thermal and hydrodynamic interactions remains unresolved. Here, a Eulerian-Lagrangian framework has been developed to address this, capturing two-way momentum, energy exchange, and nanoparticle interactions under non-isothermal conditions. We find that Brownian motion acts in two opposing ways, enhancing local particle-fluid energy exchange yet driving a thermophoretic drift away from the heated wall that strengthens as particle diameter is reduced below 100 nm. At particle volume fractions of $\phi \sim 10^{-2}$, Taylor flow departs from the Nusselt scaling with dimensionless slug length, $\tilde{L}_s$, observed for particle-free flows. This coincides with alterations to bubble topology that co-benefit nanoparticle momentum and energy exchange with the carrier fluid. Examining both Poiseuille and Taylor flow problems, we observe contrasting, often opposing dimensionless heat transport behaviours, questioning the suitability of traditionally accepted mixture approaches. This work reveals that, in the visco-inertial regime ($Re > 500$), it is the interplay of hydrodynamic, Brownian, and interfacial forces, combined with the Taylor bubble and slug flow topology, which determine positive or negative $Nu$ outcomes. Interestingly, short-range particle forces at the liquid-gas interface work synergistically with the convective motion in the slug to alter local particle concentration and energy exchanges within downstream thin film and near-wall regions. The intensity of this convective flow was found to impact both slug and film transport phenomena, improving the redistribution of nanoparticles when $\tilde{L}_s \leq 1.6$ and with increasing $Re$.

papers.title: Acoustic Scattered Field Calculation for a Moving Source Using Time-Dependent Physical Optics
papers.summary: We present a time-dependent physical optics (TDPO) formulation for computing the acoustic scattered field of a stationary object in response to a moving source in three-dimensional space. Due to the motion of the source, which may be fast, the conventional frequency-domain PO method is not employed. Instead, a time-domain variant that explicitly accounts for the motion is formulated. The study focuses on the near-field regime, where source motion induces a complex wave field beyond a simple Doppler effect. The proposed algorithm accommodates arbitrary source trajectories and arbitrary signal bandwidth, as well as high source velocities relative to the speed of sound. Near and beyond the shadow boundary, where PO is least accurate, the formulation is supplemented by a Fock correction of the surface field, extended here to a moving source with a harmonic signal. The method matches or exceeds the accuracy of finite element simulations at a computational cost lower by orders of magnitude.

papers.title: Photon-efficient readout of optical cavity arrays via spatial heterodyne
papers.summary: Optical cavity arrays are an emerging tool for efficiently interfacing optical photons to quantum emitters for applications such as quantum computing. Enabled by the improved scaling of heterodyne detection over intensity detection in the presence of technical noise, we demonstrate signal-to-noise ratio greater than one down to the single detected photon level, even in the presence of hundreds of noise equivalent photons. papers.title: The RAS-CCSD model, with applications for open-shell molecules
papers.summary: The restricted active space coupled cluster singles and doubles (RAS-CCSD) model, and its pilot implementation is detailed. papers.title: Capillary-gravity wave resistance of a translating, pulsating source
papers.summary: A disturbance in steady rectilinear translation along a capillary-gravity interface radiates waves only above a minimum speed $c_{min}$, where it experiences a wave resistance; below this threshold it generates no waves, and the response is merely a localised deformation of the interface around the source, free of wave resistance. Modulating the source amplitude at a frequency $\Omega$ shifts the forcing to the sideband pair $kV\pm\Omega$, where $k$ is the wavenumber and $V$ is the translation speed, opening resonance conditions absent from the steady problem; radiation then sets in below the steady threshold $c_{min}$. Here we derive the mean wave resistance $\langle R\rangle$ of a line source in closed form, and show it to be strictly positive at every nonzero speed $V$: the drag-free below-threshold regime disappears for any $\Omega\neq 0$. Crossing the radiation transitions---where the group velocity matches the source speed---produces integrable resonant peaks in $\langle R\rangle$, whose exponents we derive, including at the cusp where two transition branches merge. Below threshold, where a steadily moving source feels no drag, $\langle R\rangle$ rises from zero as $\Omega^5$ (at fixed $V$). Throughout, surface tension is essential to $\langle R\rangle$: because it controls the short, dominant capillary-scale waves, discarding it misrepresents $\langle R\rangle$ over almost the entire speed-frequency plane.

papers.title: Wave-driven geostrophic vortices in rotating turbulence
papers.summary: We perform direct numerical simulations of rotating turbulence to investigate the mechanisms responsible for the maintenance of large-scale geostrophic vortices. We confirm that the Reynolds stresses generated by inertial waves are consistent with the Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes balance of the large-scale flow and demonstrate the predicted cyclone-anticyclone asymmetry, with cyclones exhibiting stronger azimuthal velocities and more compact cores. Wave-field analysis provides evidence that geostrophic vortices selectively reflect and absorb inertial waves according to the sign of their angular momentum. Wave absorption occurs either through the formation of a critical layer ahead of the reflection point or through enhanced viscous dissipation associated with increasing local wavenumber. As rotation increases, fewer inertial waves undergo resonant absorption, reducing angular-momentum transfer to the vortices and weakening the geostrophic flow. Consequently, the fraction of energy contained in geostrophic modes depends non-monotonically on the rotation rate, demonstrating that sufficiently rapid rotation can ultimately suppress, rather than enhance, turbulence two-dimensionalization.

papers.title: Simultaneous Recovery of Dielectric Constants, Photoelastic Constants, and Strain Profiles from Picosecond Ultrasonic Echoes
papers.summary: Light reflected from a deforming solid depends on boundary motion and strain-induced modulation of the dielectric response. For a propagating acoustic field, scattering from different depths interferes coherently, so the measured optical amplitude and phase depend jointly on the strain profile, dielectric constant, and photoelastic constant. Optical tomography often makes such reconstructions tractable through independent projections. To probe mechanical strain, however, the optical measurement also depends on the material properties that mediate its observation, requiring those properties to be known or assumptions about the field. Here we show that broadband picosecond ultrasonic echoes in an opaque solid can supply the missing information. Fourier transformation of the measured complex relative reflectance change obtained with monochromatic light at normal incidence gives access to many acoustic frequency components. We recover the complex dielectric and photoelastic constants together with the nanoscale depth-dependent strain profile by formulating the reconstruction as a multiparameter nonlinear eigenvalue problem. We demonstrate the method using experimental echoes from a chromium film. The recovered refractive index agrees with ellipsometry, whereas the recovered strain profile closely follows a two-temperature-model prediction including electron and thermal diffusion and frequency-dependent ultrasonic attenuation. Synthetic echoes test robustness to added noise. Broadband response thus replaces additional optical projections, making the measurement self-calibrating and enabling simultaneous recovery of an unknown physical field and the material properties that mediate its optical observation.

papers.title: Transfer learning-aided, artificial intelligence approach to evaluate optical properties of materials for classical and quantum photonic applications
papers.summary: In this study, an artificial intelligence-assisted evaluation of the refractive indices of different materials is performed. The evaluation of the refractive index is necessary to design photonic devices for various classical and quantum photonic applications, and to theoretically analyse experimental results. The refractive index is one of the crucial parameters that affect the interaction of light with matter. Although the refractive index can be measured experimentally, its estimation via computational means provide the advantage of not requiring costly instrumentation, trained researchers and could avoid potential laboratory-based uncertainties. Therefore, in this study, artificial intelligence is implemented to estimate the optical constants of two types of materials, i.e., noble metals, and semiconductors. To this end, an artificial neural network is used to estimate the real and the imaginary parts of the refractive index of a specific material for various wavelengths of light. Then, the knowledge of the trained neural network is employed to initiate and train new neural networks to estimate the refractive indices of other materials. For the training of a neural network, various methods can be deployed. However, the application of the training can be a time-consuming process. A transfer learning approach is here implemented to provide a faster training solution for the problem under study. The implementation of transfer learning allows training the neural networks for a new material with higher speed or accuracy when compared to non-knowledge transfer-based training. Our results show the efficiency of the proposed technique in accurately evaluating the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index of different materials.

papers.title: Self-Adaptive Model-Order Reduction for Shock-Dominated Problems
papers.summary: Projection-based model-order reduction (MOR) offers a promising approach for accelerating expensive full-order model (FOM) by constructing reduced-order models (ROMs) that retain the majority of FOM accuracy while significantly reducing the computational cost. However, conventional static ROMs, often following offline/online training strategy, can exhibit limited predictive capability for convection-dominated problems featuring strongly evolving physics such as shocks. Adaptive ROMs emerge as a promising alternative and address such limitation by dynamically updating the low-dimensional subspace during online simulation to track locally evolving system dynamics, thereby enabling accurate predictions even for shock-dominated flows. However, such online adaptation introduces additional computational overhead, and frequent basis and sampling-point updates can substantially reduce their computational advantage relative to their static counterpart. To reconcile this tradeoff, the current work introduces a self-adaptive MOR framework that dynamically constructs and deploys the most appropriate ROM formulation (either adaptive or static) on the fly according to the evolving characteristics of the solution. to achieve optimal computational efficiency while maintaining high modeling accuracy of the local physics during the online model execution. In this regard, the proposed framework seeks to exploit the advantages of both adaptive- and static-ROM approaches to achieve an optimal computational efficiency and predictive accuracy while reducing reliance on extensive offline training. The framework is developed and evaluated for modeling rotating detonation engines (RDEs), which provide a challenging test environment involving strongly convection-dominated, transient, and multiscale reacting-flow dynamics.

papers.title: Planar intrusions from a narrow, jet-like source in a linearly stratified ambient
papers.summary: We present two and three dimensional direct numerical simulations of planar intrusions injected from a continuously supplied, narrow source into a linearly stratified ambient at the level of neutral buoyancy. The evolution passes through three phases. A laminar leading vortex dipole first advances at constant speed with a varicose wave train behind it; the trailing jet then undergoes a sinuous instability whose initial growth rate and wavelength agree with inviscid unstratified planar-jet theory evaluated on the local jet; the flow finally relaxes into a buoyancy-controlled wedge whose area grows linearly in time. Three-dimensional simulations show that the transition remains organized by the planar instability, while three-dimensionality reshapes the near-source region into a slowly evolving, actively mixing zone that entrains an additional twenty to one hundred percent of the source flux depending on source width. Rescaled with this measured effective flux, the downstream intrusion collapses reasonably well onto the similarity solution for a wide-source intrusion.

papers.title: A Shy Voter Model: Entropy Flux in Opinion Formation
papers.summary: Some voters conceal their opinions, causing a mismatch between visible and private opinions in polls. Conventional voter models do not account for such concealment. Here, we introduce a shy voter model that incorporates a hidden state in addition to two visible states, as an extension of the conventional majority-rule voter model. The model exhibits continuous and hybrid transitions, yielding a rich phase diagram organized by the hidden fraction, i.e., the fraction of voters in the hidden state. For a large hidden fraction, the system undergoes a hybrid transition from the ordered state to the symmetric (disordered) state, whereas for a small hidden fraction, it exhibits a continuous transition, with a tricritical point separating the two regimes. Near criticality, both the order-parameter variance and the susceptibility diverge. The hidden fraction also governs the entropy flux, a quantity that is not directly observable in real-world situations. Thus, opinion concealment qualitatively reshapes opinion dynamics, while the present framework provides a basis for further extensions toward more realistic forms of social interactions.

papers.title: Quantum tomography of bright squeezed vacuum via strong-field ionization
papers.summary: Strong-field physics uses intense optical fields to probe and control electron motion on ultrafast timescales. Recent advances in bright squeezed vacuum have brought macroscopic quantum states of light into the ultrafast strong-field regime, opening prospects for high-harmonic generation and photoionization. Yet linking its phase-space structure to subcycle electron dynamics remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate strong-field tunneling ionization of xenon using a phase-referenced combination of coherent and squeezed fields, with the coherent field defining the ionization clock and quadrature fluctuations of the zero-mean squeezed field providing control. The squeezed field selectively modulates atomic tunneling barriers and electron wave packets, imprinting signatures on photoelectron momentum distributions, number statistics, and energy spectra. Using coincidence measurements of photon number and phase-sensitive photoelectron momentum distributions, we perform quantum state tomography of the driving field by reconstructing its Wigner function. These results establish a bidirectional interface between quantum optics and nonperturbative strong-field electron dynamics, in which the driving quantum field shapes subcycle electron motion while photoionization provides a phase-sensitive probe of the field's quantum state. This work opens new routes toward controlling electron dynamics with quantum light and phase-sensitive quantum state metrology through ultrafast strong-field electron dynamics.

papers.title: Global Structure-Constrained 4D prestack inversion
papers.summary: Prestack seismic inversion often suffers from inherent ill-posedness and is significantly affected by complex factors such as the wavelets, parameter coupling, heterogeneous media, fault displacements, and stratigraphic variations, making it difficult for the conventional inversion methods to accurately recover subsurface information. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a global inversion method based on multi-dimensional matrix multiplication to optimize the inversion results under structure constraints. This method first represents the inversion model as a four-dimensional tensor representing spatial and parameter dimensions. By performing multi-dimensional matrix multiplication operations in various directions of the model, a multi-dimensional tensor of observed data is effectively constructed. Secondly, multi-dimensional regularization are introduced. By analyzing the impact of different dimensional constraints on the inversion results, targeted parameter selection and adjustment are achieved, significantly enhancing the stability of the inversion process and effectively suppressing noise. Finally, stratigraphic and fault constraints extracted from seismic interpretation are incorporated to improve the geological coherence and reasonableness of the inversion results. Both synthetic and field data experiments demonstrate that the proposed method effectively enhances the robustness of inversion in complex structural areas while maintaining high computational efficiency, validating its effectiveness in practical applications.

papers.title: A ghost-cell immersed boundary method for the shallow water equations on Cartesian grids: mass conservation and wetting and drying over variable topography
papers.summary: A ghost-cell immersed boundary method is proposed for the two-dimensional shallow water equations with a variable bed (topography), solved with an explicit Godunov-type finite volume scheme (unsplit second-order MUSCL, HLLC flux, hydrostatic reconstruction) on Cartesian grids. Ghost-cell methods leak mass through the wall. To find a robust and conservative treatment, eight constructions of the ghost values and a cut-cell form of the continuity equation were applied to seven test problems, which include wetting and drying on sloping beds and a laboratory dam break. In the resulting scheme, the ghost values are interpolated bilinearly at the image point; solid and dry nodes are excluded, and the weights of the remaining nodes are renormalized. Mass is conserved by solving the continuity equation in cut-cell form, while the momentum equations are left unchanged. The proposed scheme is about as accurate as the ghost-cell method without this modification and preserves a lake at rest whose shoreline crosses an immersed wall. Because only the continuity equation is modified, it avoids the treatment of the momentum equations on cut cells (wall pressure, cell merging) that a full cut-cell method requires.

papers.title: Programmable spatiotemporal shaping for partially coherent structured wave packets
papers.summary: Providing more coherent light with space-time coupling offers unprecedented opportunities across diverse scientific disciplines and areas of technology. However, in many applications, tailored laser beams with partial coherence in space and time are desired. Here, we demonstrate a programmable approach for simultaneously shaping the intensity and coherence distributions of spatiotemporally coupled partially coherent wave packets. By jointly engineering the fractal speckle of a dynamic scatterer and applying tailored modulation of the illumination function, we experimentally generate partially coherent laser beams with arbitrarily designed intensity and nontrivial coherence distributions. The proposed approach is compatible with ultrafast laser pulses, enabling the on-demand generation of partially coherent space-time wave packets. The resulting spatiotemporally partially coherent wave packets exhibit non-separable space-time intensity profiles together with engineered spatiotemporal correlation distributions. This work provides a versatile framework for tailoring partially coherent light in space and time, with varied applications in relativistic laser-matter interaction, passive imaging and optical manipulation.

papers.title: Implicit PIC Simulations of Hydrogen Plasmas with Intense Negative Ion Production
papers.summary: High-density plasma discharges in hydrogen operating at low pressures are of considerable interest for negative ion production used in many applications. Their weak collisionality requires a kinetic, nonlocal description, and a popular approach is to model such discharges numerically using the particle-in-cell (PIC) method combined with Monte Carlo collisions (MCC). However, the most commonly used explicit momentumconserving variant of this method is highly inefficient because it must resolve both the Debye length and the plasma period. In this context, the implicit energy-conserving PIC/MCC scheme appears to be an attractive alternative, as it can model the plasmas of interest using their actual parameters without resorting to artificial scaling techniques. This work considers simulations of two types of high-density plasma discharges performed using electromagnetic or electrostatic energy-conserving PIC/MCC codes in hydrogen, and discusses the observed negative ion production.

papers.title: A Low-Temperature Tool for Acousto-electric Detection
papers.summary: We have developed an apparatus for the measurement of the acousto-electric effect (AEE) from room temperature to liquid nitrogen temperatures. The AEE is excited by bulk acoustic waves (BAWs) for which a lithium niobate piezoelectric actuator is employed. A very low background noise level is realized through careful electrical and mechanical design of the setup. The validity of the setup is tested by measuring the AEE in heavily doped P-type and N-type silicon. The opposite sign of the AEE signal was seen for both samples, showing dependence of the signal on the type of charge carrier being dragged by acoustic waves. The signal showed quadratic dependence on the driving voltage, which is consistent with the AEE literature. Further, a temperature dependence of the AEE signal was measured, which exhibits a monotonic increase with a rise in temperature. The ability to probe the AEE in bulk samples at low temperatures makes this setup a promising tool to investigate the AEE and related phenomena in different materials at cryogenic temperatures.

papers.title: Relativistic Six-Fluid Rotating-Plasma Force-Balance Equilibria for p-11B Fusion Conditions in Spherical Tori
papers.summary: We formulate an axisymmetric spherical torus (ST) six-component magnetofluid equilibrium model for p_11B plasmas composed of thermal and suprathermal proton, boron, and electron fluids. The model is designed for p_11B parameter regimes where ion energies, strong current drive, energetic electron populations, and ion-electron temperature separation can render a single_fluid static_equilibrium description inadequate. It generalizes rotating_plasma equilibrium theory by incorporating relativistic thermal enthalpy corrections to the electron fluids via h(T/m_ec^2) and by constructing modified flux functions Y_{\alpha} associated with canonical angular momentum for each component {\alpha}. The equilibrium is determined by a Grad-Shafranov-like Ampere law for the poloidal magnetic flux Psi, algebraic density relations constrained by quasineutrality, and prescribed profile functions F_{\alpha}(Y_{\alpha}), T_{\alpha}(Y_{\alpha}) and K_{\alpha}(Y_{\alpha}). The manuscript includes the relativistic magnetofluid equations, the axisymmetric equilibrium formulation, the six_fluid computational method, and four numerical equilibria: two reactor_relevant ST p_11B parameter sets and two EHL-2 ST cases. The examples span toroidal beta b_T = 0.058_0.253, plasma currents I_p = 2.697_12.59 MA, and suprathermal electron temperatures T_eh = 287 keV_2.37 MeV, with h up to 19.1. Over these parameter ranges, Ampere's law accuracy, electrostatic potential accuracy, and component_resolved radial force balance can have errors ranging from 3% to below 0.1%. These results indicate that high-temperature p_11B ST equilibria can differ qualitatively from the single_fluid tokamak equilibria and require analysis of equilibrium component_resolved force balance, relativistic electron enthalpy, and explicit reproducibility diagnostics.

papers.title: Experiments on an airfoil with adjustable pitch and heave under transonic buffet leading to lock-in coupling
papers.summary: This paper presents aeroelastic experiments conducted in the ONERA S3Ch transonic wind tunnel using a supercritical OAT15A airfoil mounted on a rig allowing independent control of pitch and heave degrees of freedom (DOF). The study investigates fluid-structure interaction (FSI) mechanisms and lock-in phenomena between transonic buffet and structural modes. Aerodynamic and structural responses were monitored using steady and unsteady pressure sensors, high-speed stereoscopic Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV), accelerometers, and optical sensors. Four configurations were tested: rigid (0 DOF), pitch-only (1 DOF pitch), heave-only (1 DOF heave), and combined pitch-heave (2 DOF). The test campaign spanned selected Mach numbers, angles of attack, and structural natural frequencies for each configuration. Results show that buffet-induced lock-in occurs abruptly when the Mach number increases, but only when the pitch DOF is enabled, in both the 1-DOF pitch or 2-DOF configuration. These findings establish that pitch-buffet frequency proximity is a necessary condition for lock-in. In the 2-DOF configuration, continuous Mach number excursions revealed a three-way coupling involving the buffet, pitch, and bending modes, with the bending mode modulating the coupled dynamics. This coupling generates large-amplitude limit-cycle oscillations (LCO) within seconds, persisting over a narrow Mach range before buffet cessation.

papers.title: High Sensitivity Transient Holographic Full-Polarization Microscopy
papers.summary: The polarization state of light provides direct access to ultrafast electronic, magnetic, and structural dynamics in materials. Transient wide-field microscopy with simultaneous amplitude, phase, and polarization sensitivity enables spatially resolved measurements of these dynamics, but its sensitivity is often limited by technical noise and background fluctuations. Here, we demonstrate transient holographic full-polarization microscopy with substantially reduced instrumental noise and sensitivity approaching the shot-noise limit. We compare holographic geometries using one, two, and four reference beams and find that the single-reference configuration provides the most favourable shot-noise-limited sensitivity for the derived polarization observables. Combined with two-camera detection, it simultaneously captures both orthogonal polarization components without distributing reference photons among multiple carriers. A self-referenced noise-reduction framework combining singular value decomposition and background subtraction further suppresses correlated noise. For spatially averaged regions, the baseline noise is reduced by factors of three-sixty, enabling detection of weaker transient responses at lower excitation densities and in weakly absorbing materials.

papers.title: Fingering instability of thin films with an inclined contact line
papers.summary: The fingering instability of thin-film flow is a significant obstacle to producing uniform and stable films in industrial processes. In the framework of lubrication theory, we investigate the linear stability of a gravity-driven thin film with an inclined contact line using numerical and asymptotic methods. The contact-line singularity is regularized by imposing the Greenspan slip model. As demonstrated by the results, although the contact-line inclination slightly enhances long-wavelength instability, it significantly suppresses the growth of spanwise finite-wavelength perturbations. Moreover, the most unstable wavenumber shifts toward the long-wave region as the inclination angle increases. The inclination of the contact line introduces complex eigenvalues, leading to traveling-wave modes, in contrast to the standing-wave modes observed for horizontal contact lines. We also performed asymptotic analysis in the limit of small wavenumbers, confirming the enhanced long-wave instability. The physical mechanisms underlying these stability characteristics are elucidated, revealing that the effects of contact-line inclination come from the eigenmode distortion and additional streamwise flux.

papers.title: Towards modelling abreast to in-file transitions in small pedestrian groups
papers.summary: Pedestrians in a crowd largely walk in small groups, dyads above all, and modelling how these groups arrange themselves is a step towards realistic models of the crowd as a whole. A dyad walks side by side in a dilute crowd and one behind the other in a dense one, an abreast to in-file transition recently measured in real life across the full range of naturally occurring crowd conditions (van der Laan and Corbetta, PLOS ONE 2026). The cost-function models of dyad formation by Zanlungo and coworkers (Phys. Rev. E 2014; EPL 2015) hold the pair abreast and have no in-file minimum at any finite density. Building on them, we propose and analyse a qualitative model in which the transition appears as an effective density parameter grows: the two formations become minima that coexist over a window of densities and exchange stability within it. We quantify this transition by computing the Orientation Log-Odds $\Pi_\text{OLO}$ as predicted by the model. This paper is a first step towards quantitative models of dyads and of their formation transitions.

papers.title: Kinematic saturation of the electromagnetically-induced-transparency peak in thermal atomic vapors
papers.summary: We demonstrate that, in thermal atomic vapors, the electromagnetically-induced-transparency (EIT) transmission peak exhibits saturation. Investigating the amplitude of the velocity-selected double-resonance transmission peak-a purely kinematic effect arising from finite wavevector mismatch-we identify a threshold atomic column density Ns. For column densities N below Ns, the amplitude of the transmission peak maximum increases with column density. Once it exceeds Ns, the peak amplitude maximum remains constant, while the corresponding detuning shifts away from resonance and scales as the square root of ln(N over Ns). Furthermore, We find that the operating point for optimum photon-shot-noise-limited sensitivity deviates from that of the transmission peak maximum. Our study provides guidance for optimizing EIT readout in vapor cell and for precision measurements built upon this scheme.

papers.title: Multivariate phase-space interpretation of ensemble forecasts: A comparison of physical and AI models
papers.summary: Ensemble forecasts from the ECMWF's Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) and the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS-ENS) are compared using a multi-dimensional evaluation framework. Within this framework, the uncertainty is interpreted as the linear subspace spanned by the ensemble members in phase space, from which various geometric properties are extracted. As revealed by the analysis, the error does not entirely lie in this subspace, but is reasonably well calibrated in all directions. Moreover, the framework allows to quantify that this subspace critically depends on the number of ensemble members, suggesting that the current setups only partially represent the uncertainty subspace. This phase-space interpretation furthermore allows a direct comparison of the error-representation patterns of AIFS-ENS and IFS by computing the principal angles between the subspaces: IFS and AIFS ensemble subspaces do not entirely overlap in phase space, even though they were shown to have similar abilities to represent the amplitude and the structure of the error.

papers.title: Fading Memory and Nonlinear Dynamics in a Microring Resonator Network and their Use in Computation
papers.summary: Silicon microring resonators are promising components for photonic reservoir computing because their nonlinear optical response can transform signals and retain information about recent inputs. Under constant optical excitation, their coupled free-carrier and thermal dynamics can generate self-pulsing: a periodic output response. However, constant-input behavior does not reveal how these dynamics respond to randomly modulated signals or whether their memory is useful for temporal processing. Here, we characterize a single silicon microring resonator and a passive network of microring resonators under random input modulation. The temporal component associated with self-pulsing remains observable under random modulation, but the largest fading memory occurs near the self-pulsing boundary, where no resolved self-pulsing-like oscillation is present. reservoir computing metrics, such as memory capacity, map this accessible memory, and its decay provides effective timescales associated mainly with free-carrier and thermal relaxation. Finally, we use NARMA reconstruction to test whether the measured memory profile supports nonlinear temporal processing. Responses with a resolved self-pulsing-like component perform worse on this task, and the intrinsic memory profile is not matched to the required input history. These results show that reservoir computing metrics can characterize nonlinear microring resonator dynamics even when the physical system is not an effective standalone reservoir for the selected task.

papers.title: Asynchronous Terahertz-field sampling with soliton microcombs
papers.summary: Terahertz time-domain spectroscopy records the electric field of terahertz transients and underpins applications from materials science to non-destructive testing. Asynchronous optical sampling enables systems without moving parts, but its acquisition rate remains fundamentally limited by the repetition-rate of the driving femtosecond lasers. Here, we demonstrate asynchronous terahertz-field sampling with two chip-based soliton microcombs. Their ultrahigh 25 GHz pulse repetition-rate drastically reduces dead-time during acquisition, and stabilization via sideband injection-locking enables coherent averaging without active feedback loops. At 10 kHz acquisition rate, we achieve a dynamic range of 74 dB in a single 100 $\mu$s scan, and 100 dB after 50 ms of coherent averaging with a 1.6 THz bandwidth. Acquisition rates of up to 100 kHz are demonstrated, limited only by detection electronics. Together with a proof-of-concept silicon wafer thickness measurement, these results establish soliton microcombs as compact sources for rapid terahertz-field sampling.

papers.title: Readout chain of SPD DAQ system
papers.summary: The Spin Physics Detector (SPD) experiment at the NICA collider of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) aims to study the spin structure of the nucleon and spin-related phenomena. The experimental conditions, including the high interaction rate and the large number of readout channels, require a triggerless data acquisition system with high throughput and a scalable architecture. This work presents a hardware implementation of the readout chain that extends the previously proposed SPD DAQ architecture. The chain is based on two levels of concentrators. The L1 concentrator provides the interface between the front-end electronics and the next system level and distributes synchronous signals. The L2 concentrator aggregates data streams from several L1 concentrators before transmitting them to the computing system. A key feature of the L2 implementation is the offloading of data reception, buffering, and aggregation from the host CPU to the FPGA, motivated by the large number of small packets generated by the readout electronics. The developed hardware platforms and their operating logic are presented, together with experimental results for the main interfaces and data-path components. The obtained results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed hardware architecture and its application in a scalable SPD data acquisition system.

papers.title: Identifying Arctic states vulnerable to rapid ice loss with a convolutional neural network
papers.summary: This work investigates the incidence of rapid ice-loss events in the Arctic, in which a substantial fraction of September sea-ice is lost in only a few years. Such events are seen to occur in climate model simulations forced with increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, but not as yet in the relatively short observational record. We train a convolutional neural network (CNN) using six large climate model ensembles to diagnose vulnerability to rapid ice-loss events. The trained model is shown to separate higher and lower risk states in out-of-sample climate models via a leave-one-out cross-validation. The model emphasises the role of persistently thin sea-ice, remaining sea-ice extent and sustained high upper ocean heat content as predictors of rapid ice-loss. The CNN is applied to observational data over the satelite-era showing a signal for rapid ice-loss prior to a drop around 2007 and an increasing risk from around 2015 to present. Such rapid-ice loss events would likely have dramatic consequences for Arctic ecosystems, coastal communities and global shipping.

papers.title: Onset condition of the ramified-jet regime: an experimental and theoretical study
papers.summary: This study experimentally and theoretically investigates the electrically induced transition of a gas-focused liquid jet into a rim-emitting sheet. Ultra-high-speed imaging was used to examine the effects of applied voltage, gas and liquid flow rates, and liquid properties on sheet formation and breakup. Fully developed, quasi-stable sheets formed with ethanol, whereas isopropanol exhibited only initial sheet formation. Increasing voltage promoted sheet stretching, finer and more numerous rim jets, and a narrower spray. Higher gas flow rates shifted the transition towards the nozzle and produced finer structures, while higher liquid flow rates generated larger sheets with thicker rims. A first-order theoretical model assumes an equipotential interface and neglects finite charge relaxation, hydrodynamic perturbations, and nonlinear evolution. It balances destabilizing Maxwell-pressure perturbations against restoring capillary-pressure perturbations on a conducting cylindrical jet. The model identifies the elliptic azimuthal mode, m = 2, as the first unstable mode leading to sheet formation and predicts a critical electric Bond number of 3. Predicted onset voltages agree with measurements within 20%, and the threshold was consistent with published ramified-electrospray observations. The agreement with experiments supports electrocapillary symmetry breaking as the mechanism of onset and provides a compact, physically grounded criterion for predicting the transition from electrified jets to rim-emitting sheets.

papers.title: Bayesian Inversion Beyond the Generator's Range: Reducing Non-physical Constraints from Generative Neural Networks
papers.summary: To address non-uniqueness in geophysical inversions, Generative Neural Networks (GNNs) are often used to parameterise geological or other prior information in a lower-dimensional space (the so-called latent space), thereby reducing the number of inversion parameters. However, the training samples that represent this information are then always incorrect, because Earth structure is not intrinsically low-dimensional, and all GNNs are subject to training errors. Consequently, even when solutions are mapped back to the original higher-dimensional space, they inherit this imperfection and remain restricted to a low-dimensional manifold. From a mathematical point of view, latent space inversion thus fails fundamentally: generally, it can not even reproduce the best, higher-dimensional approximation to the true Earth. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an `escaping prior' distribution, which provides the necessary freedom to find solutions beyond the manifold of GNN-generated solutions, while still using the GNN as a guide. We use a hierarchical Bayesian approach to adapt the strength of prior information to the observed data and synthetic forward function $\textit{a posteriori}$. We illustrate our method on low-dimensional problems where the escaping prior is defined over a 1D manifold in 2D space. We then compare our approach with standard latent space and model space inversions using a uniform prior distribution in synthetic tomography problems, ranging from simple to more geologically realistic cases. Furthermore, we tested scenarios where the true solution is either far from or close to the manifold. In each case, our escaping prior shows significantly better results than the alternatives. It results in solutions beyond each GNN's generative capabilities, solutions which include the best possible model, and clearly demonstrates the limitations of latent space inversion.

papers.title: Single-electron Fluorine Bonding. I. The SEFB-15 and CSFB-14 Benchmark Datasets, Reference Binding Energies and Intermolecular Bond Distances: Assessment of M06-2X density functional
papers.summary: Halogen bonding in which a covalently bound fluorine acts as halogen-bond donor (F-bonding) is rare, and its open-shell variant with radical electron donors remains unexplored. We introduce SEFB-15 dataset (15 open-shell DF$\cdots$CH$_3$ complexes) exemplifying single-electron F-bonding (SEFB) and CSFB-14 dataset (14 closed-shell DF$\cdots$NH$_3$ complexes) representing closed-shell F-bonding (CSFB). Reference binding energies (BEs) at DF-RMP2-F12/CBS//DF-RMP2-F12/VDZ-F12 are validated against CCSD(T), CCSD(T)-F12b, W1-F12 and W2-F12 for selected systems (DF = F$_2$, NCF, CNF, NH$_3$F$^+$ and NH$_2$F$_2^+$), with MA%D of 4.5% (DF$\cdots$CH$_3$) and 3.4% (DF$\cdots$NH$_3$) against CCSD(T)-F12b/CBS//CCSD(T)-F12b/VDZ-F12. BEs from W1-F12 and W2-F12 are identical. Reference F-bond distances at DF-RMP2-F12/VDZ-F12 are validated against CCSD(T)-F12b, CCSD(T), CCSD, and DCSD for the same systems, with MA%D of 0.9% (SEFB) and 0.4% (CSFB) against CCSD(T)-F12b/VDZ-F12. M06-2X is recommended for closed-shell halogen bonding with heavier halogens but has never been assessed for open-shell F-bonding. M06-2X/AVTZ systematically overbinds all SEFB-15 complexes and underestimates their F-bond distances, with MA%Ds of 75.8% on BEs and 8.9% on F-bond distances. M06-2X predicts comparable BEs for F$_2\cdots$CH$_3$ and F$_2\cdots$NH$_3$, contrary to all ab initio results, an anomaly persisting across all 16 basis sets. Neither basis set nor BSSE correction resolves the overbinding. BSSE correction worsens BEs for DF$\cdots$NH$_3$ complexes. For CSFB-14, M06-2X/AVTZ yields MA%Ds of 16.0% for BEs and 3.3% for F-bond distances. M06-2X is reliable for CSFB but unreliable for SEFB regardless of basis set. Companion paper II reports performance of other Minnesota functionals and ab initio methods for these datasets.

papers.title: Forecasting carbon-risk hotspots ahead of the extreme 2026 El Ni\~no
papers.summary: A potentially super El Ni\~no is forecasted in 2026, raising the need to anticipate land carbon-cycle risks before its impacts unfold. Forecasts indicate a $0.23 \pm 0.21$ PgC reduction in global net biome productivity in the second half of 2026, with hotspots of sink weakening in eastern South America and elevated fire risk in Southeast Asia.

papers.title: Versatile two-layer model for thermohydraulic prediction of microchannel heat sinks
papers.summary: Three-dimensional conjugate heat-transfer simulations provide detailed predictions for microchannel heat sinks but can be computationally demanding when many geometries and operating conditions are evaluated. This study develops a versatile two-layer model (VTLM) that reduces the three-dimensional problem to two coupled two-dimensional fields while retaining the in-plane geometry of the flow passages and fins. Effects associated with the unresolved channel-height direction are incorporated through hydraulic and thermal closures that account for wall friction and the fluid- and fin-side contributions to interlayer heat transfer. The closures are evaluated from the representative channel geometry, flow-development condition, and fin configuration. The VTLM was assessed against three-dimensional reference models across broad ranges of channel aspect ratios and operating conditions, including uniform and nonuniform fin arrangements. Compared with the existing two-layer models, the VTLM showed improved overall agreement with the three-dimensional reference results. The results showed that prediction accuracy was governed mainly by the flow-development condition and channel aspect ratio, from which a conservative screening guideline was proposed for the examined straight-channel configurations. The assessment of finned expansion--contraction channels further supported the applicability of the VTLM to the investigated passages with abrupt width changes. Overall, the VTLM provides a reduced-dimensional framework for thermohydraulic analysis across the range of microchannel heat-sink configurations examined in this study without explicitly resolving the channel-height direction.

papers.title: Finite-event modulation transfer through forward-scattering media
papers.summary: How spatial structure is transferred through a forward-scattering medium depends jointly on pattern scale and propagation distance. Starting from photon exit displacements, we derive modulation transfer while retaining the number, depths, and projected angles of individual deflections, with event occurrences described by a homogeneous Poisson process along the propagation path. The second angular moment yields a leading low-frequency loss proportional to $k^2z^3$, where $k$ is angular spatial frequency and $z$ is thickness. At finite frequency, the model predicts two coupled departures: loss bends below its low-frequency quadratic extrapolation at fixed thickness, and transfer curves separate by thickness at fixed $k^2z^3$. The leading corrections to both effects arise from the same fourth angular moment. For symmetric, nondegenerate projected-angle distributions, the full response further establishes increasing loss with thickness in the same medium at fixed joint variable. Binary-pattern measurements through TiO$_2$ suspensions span five nominal loadings, seven thicknesses, and 20 spatial frequencies, supporting the approximate low-frequency scaling and showing both departures. A Gaussian effective-angle response calibrated only on lower-frequency data predicts the held-out higher-frequency band without refitting, with a logarithmic root-mean-square error of 0.0181 compared with 0.1021 for quadratic extrapolation. The results show that finite-event statistics provide a common physical origin for spectral bending and thickness-dependent departure from low-frequency scaling, linking coarse-pattern transport to finer spatial structure.

papers.title: Cavity-modified static polarizabilities of atoms and small molecules within QED full configuration interaction
papers.summary: Static dipole polarizabilities of H$_2$, LiH, and helium confined in a single-mode optical cavity are computed using quantum-electrodynamical full configuration interaction (QED-FCI). Response properties are obtained as finite-field derivatives of the coupled electron-photon energy. The cavity-induced modification is found to arise from the competition of two contributions of opposite sign, the dipole self-energy and photon exchange, whose relative strength depends on both the cavity frequency and the number of photons involved in the exchange. The residual change suppresses the response of the molecular ground electronic states. For the metastable states of helium atom this balance changes qualitatively, and the differential response of the $2\,^3S_1 \to 2\,^1S_0$ clock transition, which governs its sensitivity to static electric fields and to thermal radiation, is strongly enhanced instead. Cavity confinement can therefore either reduce or increase the dc Stark and blackbody-radiation shifts of a frequency standard, depending on the electronic structure of the states involved. The reported data serve as a reference for cavity-modified response and underscore the need for an exact treatment of light-matter correlation in cavity-QED predictions.

papers.title: Exact Gaussian--Hermite closure of the mapping quantum--classical Liouville equation
papers.summary: Liouville equation contains an excess coupling term in addition to the Poisson bracket. Neglecting this term yields the Poisson bracket mapping equation (PBME). We expand the mapping dependence of the density in Hermite functions about the Gaussian factor common to all physical mapping densities. In this basis, the excess coupling term acts purely as a raising operator and exactly cancels the raising contribution generated by the back--reaction force. Consequently, the exact dynamics does not generate higher Hermite orders and closes on a finite, sparse system of equations for the coefficient fields. Within the physical sector, these equations reduce to the subsystem quantum--classical Liouville equation. In contrast, the PBME retains the raising contribution of the force, modifying the back reaction within the physical sector while continuously generating higher Hermite orders. For Tully's dual avoided crossing model, direct propagation of the coefficient equations confirms this finite closure and agrees with independent solutions of the subsystem equation. Comparison with converged full quantum dynamics further shows that, across all regimes examined, the PBME is less accurate than the quantum--classical description for populations, coherences, and momentum distributions.

papers.title: QUARZ: a quasi-static particle-in-cell code with non-uniform radial grids for plasma wakefields
papers.summary: We present a quasi-static particle-in-cell scheme for beam-driven plasma wakefields in cylindrical geometry that works on an arbitrary non-uniform radial grid. The field equations are discretized with hat-function finite elements and conservative finite volumes on any monotone set of radial nodes, and the transverse magnetic field is obtained explicitly, without iterations, following Baxevanis and Stupakov. An optional azimuthal mode $m=1$ describes beam offsets, tilts and hosing. The discretization keeps the discrete Gauss law exact, deposits a uniform plasma exactly on every node including the axis, and remains second-order accurate on smoothly stretched grids. Resolution can therefore be placed where the physics needs it. For a tightly focused witness beam that pulls the plasma ions onto the axis, a grid that is fine only near the axis gives the same near-axis fields as a uniform grid with the same axis resolution, with thirty times fewer cells and in thirty times less computing time. Such a grid also resolves the singular closure of a cold-plasma bubble, which a uniform grid hides by smoothing it over one cell; smoothing the plasma sources over a fixed length, chosen independently of the grid, regularizes the closure and makes the wake behind it converge. The scheme is implemented in the open-source C++/Kokkos code QUARZ (Quasistatic Arbitrary-resolution RZ), which runs on CPUs and GPUs and uses MPI with a pipelined decomposition along the co-moving coordinate. Simulations of the self-modulation of the AWAKE proton bunch agree with the three-dimensional code HiPACE++. QUARZ is, to our knowledge, the first production-grade simulation code in plasma physics that is \emph{zero-touch}: all of its source code, tests and documentation were written by an AI agent directed by a physicist who did not write a single line of the code.

papers.title: Second-order fluids and the choice of objective derivative
papers.summary: We generalize the second-order fluid constitutive model to accommodate a range of possible frame indifferent time derivatives. Using the Gordon--Schowalter derivative, which contains the upper-convected, lower-convected, and corotational (Jaumann-Zaremba) derivatives as subsets, we show how the subjective choice of derivative may change model predictions and we identify features that remain universal independent of this choice. Writing these models in terms of generic coefficients is non-universal and may lead to misinterpretations of flow predictions. However, writing the models in terms of zero-shear material functions or terminal relaxation time reveals universal and robust representations.

papers.title: Foundations for a Lens of Quantum Governance
papers.summary: The second quantum revolution is a revolution of information. Advances in quantum computation, communication, and sensing offer new capabilities while raising questions about how quantum infrastructures will be organised, accessed, and governed. We argue that their significance for governance lies not in transforming political principles, but in how their technical and infrastructural requirements may affect existing relationships of authority, responsibility, legitimacy, and power. This paper develops a quantum governance lens that connects governance scholarship with quantum information science, examining interactions between technical design, institutional arrangements, and infrastructural dependencies. We apply this lens to five areas: quantum computation, quantum key distribution, Quantum Byzantine Agreement, blind quantum computation, and dual-use quantum sensing. These applications illustrate how technical capabilities may influence access, trust, privacy, oversight, and accountability, while demonstrating that technical guarantees cannot resolve institutional questions independently. We conclude that quantum technologies do not necessarily introduce unique governance challenges or require entirely new governance frameworks. Rather, they provide a context in which established questions of legitimacy, accountability, and equity must be reconsidered in relation to emerging technological capabilities and institutional choices.

papers.title: Wireless Energy Transfer for Space Applications: A Review of Technologies, Mission Architectures, Energy Routing, and System Integration
papers.summary: Wireless energy transfer (WET) decouples energy generation from energy use, offering strategic advantages for distributed spacecraft, lunar surface networks, mobile assets, and high-power remote loads. This review organizes the field along four axes: physical mechanism, energy reference plane, mission architecture, and evidence maturity. It examines near field inductive and resonant transfer, microwave and millimeter wave power beaming, optical and laser-based transfer, space-based solar power, lunar and cislunar energy delivery, inter-spacecraft power sharing, intraspacecraft contactless interfaces, and reconfigurable or relay assisted routing within a common R0,R7 energy-accounting framework. Three conclusions emerge. First, WET is most valuable when spatial or temporal mismatches separate energy generation from load demand; it does not universally replace local generation or onboard storage. Second, dominant losses vary across system architectures. Beam collection, rectification, receiver output, and useful load efficiencies are therefore not directly comparable without explicitly defined energy reference planes. Third, technological maturity is uneven. High power ground demonstrations and short range flight applications are relatively well established, whereas long-range radiative inter spacecraft transfer, spaceborne routing hardware, lunar energy networks, and deep space applications remain supported primarily by models, simulations, and mission studies rather than hardware demonstrations. Progress requires validated end to end energy budgets under mission realistic constraints, including pointing and tracking, thermal management, environmental exposure, reliability, energy storage, and regulatory compliance.
