papers.title: Time-Resolved Phonon Dispersions of Thermally Excited Graphite at the Nanoscale
papers.summary: Lattice vibrations govern the propagation of heat in materials, and investigating their dynamics through time-resolved phonon dispersion measurements would provide insight into these excitations and their interactions. However, time-resolved measurements that directly resolve the phonon dispersion at the nanoscale have not been previously demonstrated. Momentum-resolved vibrational electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) provides access to phonon energies and momenta with nanoscale spatial resolution. Here, we combine momentum-resolved vibrational EELS with pulsed laser heating and synchronised gated electron detection to observe the phonon dispersion of graphite during controlled heating and cooling on the microsecond timescale. Recording both the gain and loss spectra at defined times relative to laser excitation, we determine the temperature at each time delay and follow changes to the phonon branches as a function of temperature. The momentum-resolved spectra reveal a decrease in energy of the optical phonon branch with increasing temperature accompanied by an increase in peak width. These changes are consistent with temperature-dependent phonon renormalisation and scattering associated with anharmonic interactions. The approach is compatible with detector gating on timescales down to 50 ns, providing a route towards extending these measurements to faster dynamics. This work demonstrates time-resolved phonon dispersion spectroscopy using vibrational EELS and provides a route towards probing temperature-dependent phonon dynamics at the nanoscale with simultaneous energy and momentum resolution.

papers.title: Exact Microscopic One-Body Reduction in the Symmetric Exclusion Process
papers.summary: The symmetric exclusion process (SEP) is a paradigmatic model of interacting particle transport. Its current--density correlations are governed by an infinite many-body hierarchy of equations. Only recently, this hierarchy was found to collapse at large scales onto a single closed equation. Is this remarkable simplification created by coarse graining, or does it reflect a deeper property already present in the microscopic dynamics? Here we show that the second scenario is realized. At arbitrary time on the lattice, the entire hierarchy collapses onto a single linear equation which is exactly equivalent to a persistence problem for a single auxiliary random walker. Thus an interacting many-body problem reduces exactly to a genuine one-body problem before any scaling limit is taken. This reduction determines the complete finite-time correlation profile, including during nonequilibrium relaxation. More broadly, the microscopic operator uncovered here opens a route to more general correlation functions in the SEP, and may point to a general organizing principle for nonequilibrium interacting particle systems.

papers.title: Momentum conservation for ab initio calculations with pseudopotentials via a phase space electronic structure formulation
papers.summary: We demonstrate how to build a robust phase space electronic Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_\text{PS}(\boldsymbol{R},\boldsymbol{P})$ that depends on nuclear position $\boldsymbol{R}$ and nuclear momentum $\boldsymbol{P}$ in the presence of ionic pseudopotentials. In particular, we show that in order to account for the non-local component of a pseudopotential while also conserving linear and angular momentum, one is forced to introduce a non-local one-electron operator $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}^\text{nl}$ that couples electronic and nuclear momenta together. To test the validity of our ansatz, we derive a generalized form of Nafie's exact equality (which relates electronic momentum and electronic position) so as to include the presence of pseudopotentials. We then benchmark our proposed phase space electronic structure theory against this generalized Nafie-like result for a diverse set of diatomic molecules spanning a wide range of elements. We find excellent agreement across this ab initio test set, highlighting the strength of our method in capturing meaningful electronic momentum beyond the Born-Oppenheimer framework.

papers.title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites
papers.summary: Double perovskites (DPs) offer a compositionally versatile platform for photocatalysis and optoelectronics, but their soft lattices favor strong exciton-phonon coupling and self-trapped excitons (STEs), which produce broad, red-shifted photoluminescence (PL). Here, we combine optical spectroscopy and ab initio calculations to study lead-free, Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals with B-site alloying from Na to K. Alloying tunes the PL energy from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV, while absorption features near 3.8 eV remain nearly unchanged. Calculations reveal that Sb doping enables bright radiative recombination channels and delocalizes the excitonic wavefunction. We identify STEs responsible for the large PL red shift, associated with an upward shift of dopant-hybridized in-gap states. Na-to-K substitution selectively changes the STE lattice distortion, explaining why PL varies strongly with composition while absorption does not. Theory further predicts pronounced PL polarization anisotropy that reflects the STE wavefunction's spatial structure and depends on B-site composition. Time-resolved anisotropy measurements closely agree with these predictions, providing experimental fingerprints of the excitonic wavefunction and its evolution with alloying. Together, these results disentangle the roles of doping and alloying in lead-free DPs and establish polarization-resolved spectroscopy as a probe of STE wavefunctions.

papers.title: Superexchange coupling between a dilute Gd3+ probe and orphan spins in a valence-bond glass
papers.summary: The valence-bond-glass state of the 4d^1 double perovskite Ba2YMoO6 combines Mo^5+ singlets with residual paramagnetic "orphan" spins whose coupling is hard to reach with bulk probes. We probe them by electron paramagnetic resonance of a dilute Gd^3+ ion on the Y^3+ site via broadband coplanar-waveguide transmission at 5 K. The isostructural nonmagnetic niobate Ba2YNbO6, doped with the same Gd^3+ probe, is a fixed-lattice control. The Gd^3+ linewidth nearly doubles in the magnetic host. Dipolar coupling to the sparse orphans is nearly an order of magnitude too weak; the excess is instead reproduced by a transferred f-d superexchange of J ~ 0.2 K, so the width is a static measure of orphan-spin coupling. The half-field (Delta m_S = +/-2) satellite collapses in the magnetic host, a dynamical dephasing channel, while the unchanged g-factor marks a zero-mean random internal field. Together the two channels probe the coupling and dynamics of valence-bond-glass orphan spins.

papers.title: Competing delocalisation and localisation induced by the dipolar tail in fragmented lattice gases
papers.summary: We investigate how the long-range tail of dipole-dipole interactions modifies the dynamics of strongly interacting hard-core bosons in a one-dimensional lattice. In the nearest-neighbour model, large interactions generate an emergent Hilbert-space fragmentation into manifolds labelled by the number of nearest-neighbour bonds \(N_{\mathrm{NN}}\). The dipolar tail has a non-monotonic effect on this fragmented dynamics as the interaction-to-tunnelling ratio \(V/t\) is increased. At intermediate \(V/t\), it enhances delocalisation relative to the nearest-neighbour model by reducing the energetic detuning between neighbouring \(N_{\mathrm{NN}}\) manifolds and sustaining their hybridisation by hopping. At larger \(V/t\), the same tail lifts degeneracies within each manifold, beginning with the splitting associated with the next-nearest-neighbour bond number \(N_{\mathrm{NNN}}\), and promotes intra-manifold localisation and Hilbert-space shattering. The competition between these two effects produces a crossover from a delocalising to a localising role of the dipolar tail, visible in the late-time spatial inhomogeneity. This crossover occurs for nearly all initial states considered and persists at different fillings. Transverse confinement strengthens the short-range part of the dipolar tail and shifts the crossover to lower \(V/t\), bringing it into the regime relevant to current experiments with magnetic atoms and polar molecules.

papers.title: Spin textures at the Fermi surface of ferromagnets and associated torque
papers.summary: We establish theoretically that transverse spin textures are generically induced by the spin-orbit interaction at the Fermi surface of centrosymmetric ferromagnetic metals. We confirm this prediction with {\em ab initio} computations for Fe, Co and Ni. By symmetry, this cannot be associated with spin-orbit torques under a uniform current. However, a new {\em current-gradient-induced} torque emerges in nanoscale geometries. For a series of Ni-based bilayers, the computed Ni thickness dependence of the current-gradient-induced torque is in quantitative agreement with measurements previously attributed to orbital torques. We discuss how this opens a new avenue for the electrical control of magnetic orders, possibly also including the N\'eel vector of metallic altermagnets.

papers.title: Towards synergy between theory and experiments: First-passage processes under resetting with stochastic return protocols
papers.summary: Stochastic resetting with stochastic return (SR) has recently emerged as an effective and practically relevant strategy for controlling first-passage phenomena and optimizing search processes by significantly reducing completion times in a wide class of stochastic systems. While most theoretical studies assume instantaneous return (IR), in realistic systems the return to the resetting position typically occurs over a finite time. We consider a 1-d diffusing particle in a harmonic trap with stiffnesses $k_1$ and $k_2$ during search and return, respectively. The particle searches for the target and, upon resetting at rate $r$, enters the return phase, continuing until it reaches either the origin or the absorbing target at $L>0$. Notably, the model permits target detection throughout the return phase, distinguishing it from IR scenarios. We analytically derive the MFPT for our model and determine parameter regions where SR enhances or suppresses search efficiency over the underlying dynamics, constructing the corresponding phase diagram using the coefficient of variation criterion. We further identify regimes in which SR is more efficient than IR using the SR criterion. This behavior is tested across different parameter sets taken from experimental studies by Goerlich et al., Biroli et al., and Besga et al. We map the parameter values reported in existing experimental studies onto our theoretical phase diagram, thereby identifying the regimes in which SR outperforms IR. In particular, we find that the most relevant region of the phase space, where SR is most beneficial corresponds to larger values of the potential strength in the search phase and lower values of potential in the return phase. Our results provide experimentally testable predictions and bridge the gap between theoretical resetting models and optical trap mediated finite-time return dynamics.

papers.title: Single anyons and anyon binding in a quantum Hall dot
papers.summary: Anyons are particles with quantized fractional statistics. In theory, a single anyon can be stabilized as a localized fractional charge within the bulk of a topologically ordered two-dimensional insulator. However, experiments to date have focused on probing anyons in structures in which many anyonic excitations coexist and interact. Here, we demonstrate the trapping of a single anyon in a device consisting of a graphene-based quantum point contact with an embedded tunable quantum Hall dot. Benchmarking our device at v = 1, we demonstrate backscattering between Fermi liquid edge states mediated by the whole-electron Coulomb blockade of the dot. The cleanliness and control available in our device allow depletion of the dot to the last quasihole, and we observe spin blockade for transitions to the opposite-spin Landau level. At v = 1/3 and 2/3, we observe backscattering resonances with three times the frequency, consistent with resonant transmission of e/3 charges via a single anyon transistor. We demonstrate controlled depletion to the last quasiparticle to form a single anyon quantum dot. Tracing the charge addition spectrum for quasiparticle number Nqp = 1-5, we observe highly irregular addition energies, consistent with DMRG modeling showing a complex orbital shell-filling behavior. At higher Nqp = 10-20, the addition energies show a striking pattern: quasiholes at 1/3 (and quasiparticles at 2/3) show a regular addition spectrum while quasiparticles at 1/3 (and quasiholes at 2/3) do not. We trace the origin of this irregularity to an attractive component of the inter-anyon interaction: by experimentally tuning the confining energy, we observe complete suppression of alternating charge sectors, after which the dot charges in increments of twice the fundamental charge. This observation indicates the emergence of an anyon binding energy as large as the charging energy.

papers.title: A hierarchy of exact lower bounds on the Laughlin spectral gap
papers.summary: We develop a bootstrap approach to deriving lower bounds on the spectral gap of the first Haldane pseudopotential Hamiltonian on the sphere with $N_\Phi$ flux quanta for arbitrary $N_\Phi$, including in the thermodynamic limit $N_\Phi \to \infty$. Our approach can in principle be generalized to pseudopotentials describing other model wavefunctions such as the Moore-Read state or Read-Rezayi sequence. Our approach is based on Knabe's observation that if $H$ is a Hamiltonian with ground state energy $0$ then the spectral gap is at least $\epsilon > 0$ if and only if $H^2 \succeq \epsilon H$. To show this inequality, we split $H^2$ into two parts, one that can be analytically bounded and another that can be bounded using a finite semidefinite program (SDP). Crucially, the size of this program is determined only by cutoff parameters, and the program depends on $N_\Phi$ only parametrically, allowing us to obtain numerically exact (up to solver precision) lower bounds on the gap. In order to turn these numerical bounds into mathematically rigorous bounds, we introduce an algorithm that can produce nearly-optimal exact feasible points for large rational SDPs. We additionally provide an algorithm that establishes the rank stability of the semidefinite program in the limit $N_\Phi \to \infty$ which is needed to certify the bound in the thermodynamic limit. Beyond establishing the Laughlin gap and revealing a potential method for deriving spectral gap lower bounds for other pseudopotentials, our work provides a general method for turning numerical semidefinite programming bounds into rigorous mathematical proofs, which may have wide applicability.

papers.title: Twofold Symmetry Observed in Bi$_{2}$Te$_{3}$/FeTe Interfacial Superconductor
papers.summary: Superconducting pairing symmetry are crucial in understanding the microscopic superconducting mechanism of a superconductor. Here we report the observation of a twofold superconducting gap symmetry in an interfacial superconductor Bi$_{2}$Te$_{3}$/FeTe, by employing quasiparticle interference (QPI) technique in scanning tunneling microscopy and macroscopic magnetoresistance measurements. The QPI patterns corresponding to energies inside and outside the gap reveal a clear anisotropic superconducting gap. Furthermore, both the in-plane angle-dependent magnetoresistance and in-plane upper critical field exhibit a clear twofold symmetry. This twofold symmetry align with the Te-Te direction in FeTe, which weakens the possible generation by bi-collinear antiferromagnetism order. Our finding provides key information in further understanding of the topological properties in Bi$_{2}$Te$_{3}$/FeTe superconducting system and propels further theoretical interests in the paring mechanism in the system.

papers.title: Revisiting magnetoelectric response in collinear antiferromagnetic zigzag chains: A downfolding approach beyond conventional low-energy models
papers.summary: Magnetoelectric (ME) effects in antiferromagnets provide a fertile platform for exploring symmetry-driven cross-correlated responses. However, their microscopic origin remains elusive and is often obscured in simplified low-energy descriptions. In this study, we revisit the microscopic mechanism of the ME effect in a collinear antiferromagnetic zigzag chain by employing a multi-orbital tight-binding model that explicitly includes both $s$- and $p$-orbital degrees of freedom. Using analytical and numerical calculations based on the Kubo formula, we demonstrate that the ME response is governed by orbital degrees of freedom activated through $s$--$p$ hybridization, while the spin contribution vanishes due to spin conservation. To elucidate the low-energy description, we derive an effective Hamiltonian projected onto the $s$-orbital subspace using the Schur complement. We show that a naive application of the Kubo formula within this effective model fails to capture the ME response. This issue is resolved by systematically incorporating vertex corrections in terms of orbital hybridization into the response functions. Furthermore, by introducing a quasiparticle renormalization scheme, we formulate a renormalized Kubo formula that preserves conservation laws and accurately reproduces the full multi-orbital results. Our analysis revisits the conventional low-energy perspective and reveals that the ME effect originates from virtual interorbital processes encoded in vertex corrections, rather than from the bare low-energy Hamiltonian. The effective framework developed here provides a unified microscopic understanding of orbital-driven ME responses and offers a systematic route to incorporate hybridization effects beyond simple low-energy models.

papers.title: Tracking Coupled Granular Temperature and Entropy Dynamics in Granular Materials via Dielectric Spectroscopy
papers.summary: In glass-forming liquids, structural dynamics are governed by configurational entropy and temperature, with dielectric relaxation time scaling alongside structural relaxation time as described by the Adam-Gibbs (AG) model. Under Edwards's athermal statistical thermodynamics, a modified AG law similarly governs granular matter, provided that granular temperature and configurational entropy are appropriately defined. This study investigates whether variations in the structural relaxation of granular systems can be probed via thermally activated processes, specifically electric charge hopping and trapping. By progressively reducing the volume of graphite powder to vary its packing fraction, we estimated relative configurational entropy and granular temperature from volumetric data, while evaluating electrical conductivity and capacity via impedance spectroscopy. We demonstrate that the logarithm of the dielectric relaxation time, derived from complex impedance, scales with granular temperature and entropy across both loose and compact states. Consequently, changes in the complex impedance resulting from packing fraction variations are tuned by granule configuration, strictly adhering to an AG-like relationship for thermal systems. These findings establish dielectric spectroscopy as a viable, non-destructive tool for tracing configurational dynamics in granular matter, analogous to its established use in polymers and glass formers.

papers.title: Composite Fermion Theory of Fractional Chern Insulators in Rhombohedral Graphene
papers.summary: The experimental observation of the fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect in rhombohedral graphene multilayers has raised questions about the nature of the fractional Chern insulator (FCI) states and the role of the moir\'e potential. In this Letter we develop a composite fermion (CF) description and discuss how moir\'e modulation and Coulomb interactions stabilize the FCI ground states. Under a flux-attachment transformation and mean-field approximation, the CF spectrum forms Landau levels that are further split by the moir\'e potential. At moir\'e filling fractions in the Jain sequence, an integer number of CF bands are occupied, resulting in an incompressible ground state with fractionally quantized Hall response. Remarkably, when the attached flux opposes the Berry curvature of the conduction band of rhombohedral graphene, the CF Landau levels are widely spaced in energy and delocalized across layers, leading to a reduced density of states that helps protect the CF mean-field state and amplifying effects of the moir\'e potential acting on the layer away from the doped electrons. Interactions between CFs further enlarge the moir\'e-induced band gap and stabilize the FCI ground state. Our work sheds light on the nature of the FCI states in rhombohedral graphene and provides a new theoretical framework for further studies.

papers.title: A clarification of Fermi's formula for the maximum of partial sums
papers.summary: In Fermi's 1926 note, the expression assigned to the probability that all partial sums remain below a threshold is the complementary crossing probability. We obtain the correct probability from the same diffusion equation and locate the inconsistency in the final integration. We then state the limit for independent increments under the Lindeberg condition. A counterexample with smooth densities shows that small individual variances do not suffice to justify this limit. The probabilistic results are classical; the purpose of this note is to reconcile the stated event with the printed calculation and to make the sufficient hypotheses for the discrete limit explicit.

papers.title: Almost invariant subspaces in the topologically non-trivial setting: a pedestrian approach
papers.summary: We present a self-contained, algorithmic construction of almost invariant subspaces [Panati et al. (2003), De Nittis and Panati (2010), Freund and Teufel (2016)] for Hofstadter-like Hamiltonians $H_b $ acting on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^2,\mathbb{C}^n)$. More precisely, for rational values of $b_0/(2\pi)$ we describe an iterative procedure that takes a ``locally gapped" projection $P_{0}$ (possibly topologically non-trivial) which commutes with $H_{b_0}$, into a projection $P_{\varepsilon}$ that commutes with $H_{b_0+\varepsilon}$ up to an error of order $\varepsilon^\infty$. Our construction insures that the Chern number of $P_{\varepsilon}$ equals the Chern number of $P_0$ as long as $P_\varepsilon$ exists. Moreover, its integrated density of states varies linearly with $\varepsilon$ (the ``St\v{r}eda formula"). We also show that any spatially localized Parseval frame of $P_{0}$ can be mapped into to a localized Parseval frame of $P_{\varepsilon}$. We choose to work with a discrete model in order to keep the technicalities to a minimum level, with no need for advanced pseudo-differential calculus. Nevertheless, we are confident that most of our results can be extended to (unbounded) magnetic (pseudo)differential operators, but the technical burden would be much heavier. This is left for future work.

papers.title: Asymmetric $q$-Gaussian Distributions from Tsallis Maximum Entropy
papers.summary: Within the framework of non-extensive statistical mechanics, $q$-Gaussian distributions arise as maximum-entropy solutions of Tsallis entropy under suitable escort moment constraints. Although widely used in physics, biology, geology, finance, and related fields, standard $q$-Gaussians are intrinsically symmetric and cannot capture asymmetric fluctuations often observed in empirical data. We ask whether asymmetry can arise from the Tsallis maximum-entropy principle without externally skewing or joining distributions. We show that this is achieved by retaining the Tsallis entropy and imposing a global escort mean together with distinct downside and upside escort semi-variances. The key step is to reformulate the problem of maximum Tsallis entropy in terms of the escort density. The nonlinear escort constraints then become affine, while maximizing Tsallis entropy becomes equivalent to maximizing a strictly concave functional over a convex feasible set. Consequently, any admissible stationary solution is the unique global maximizer of the corresponding variational problem. The finite-sample approximation properties of the proposed asymmetric $q$-Gaussian are studied through Monte Carlo experiments using synthetic data generated from Azzalini skew-Student distributions. Compared with the classical symmetric $q$-Gaussian, the asymmetric specification systematically provides a closer approximation to synthetic asymmetric heavy-tailed distributions. Finally, we fit the model to return series from major equity indices, a commodity, and cryptocurrencies, and compare its in-sample goodness of fit with that of a symmetric $q$-Gaussian. The results show that the asymmetric model offers a closer in-sample description of unconditional return distributions, most clearly in the tails.

papers.title: Free energy of non-convex multi-species Ising spin glasses with external fields
papers.summary: We identify the limit free energy of mean-field multi-species spin glasses with +/-1 spins, allowing for the presence of external fields, and without assuming any convexity property of the covariance function of the Hamiltonian. The limit is given by an "uninverted" variational formula over Brownian martingales. The proof consists in first identifying the limit free energy of configurations with a fixed magnetization. Once the magnetization is fixed, we can show the convergence of the enriched free energy to the solution of a Hamilton-Jacobi equation. The magnetization constraint is also used to show the convexity of the initial condition in this equation, and this yields a variational representation of the solution, as a Hopf formula. Convex duality then turns this formula into an optimization over martingales whose initial values are the prescribed magnetizations.

papers.title: Fermion-fermion interaction driven phase transitions in rhombohedral trilayer graphene
papers.summary: The effects of short-range fermion-fermion interactions on the low-energy properties of rhombohedral trilayer graphene are comprehensively investigated using the momentum-shell renormalization group method. We take into account all one-loop corrections and establish the energy-dependent coupled evolutions of independent fermionic couplings that carry the physical information stemming from the interplay of various fermion-fermion interactions. With detailed numerical analysis, we observe that the ferocious competition among all fermion-fermion interactions can drive fermionic couplings to four distinct fixed points, dubbed $\textrm{FP}_{1}$, $\textrm{FP}_{2}$, $\textrm{FP}_{3}$, and $\textrm{FP}_{4}$, in the interaction-parameter space. These fixed points primarily dictate the fate of the system in the low-energy regime and are always associated with some instabilities characterized by specific symmetry breakings, leading to certain phase transitions. To determine the favorable states arising from the potential phase transitions, we introduce a number of fermion-bilinear source terms to characterize the underlying candidate states. By comparing their related susceptibilities, we find that the dominant states correspond to spin-singlet superconductivity, spin-triplet pair-density-waves, and spin-triplet superconductivity for fixed points $\textrm{FP}_{1,3}$, $\textrm{FP}_{2}$, and $\textrm{FP}_{4}$, respectively. These provide valuable insights into the low-energy properties of rhombohedral trilayer graphene and analogous materials.

papers.title: Ring states in topological materials
papers.summary: Ingap states in semiconductors are commonly characterized by hydrogenic models within the effective mass approximation. However, when impurities are strong, this description fails. The bound states are non-perturbative with energy pinned to a zero of the impurity-projected Green's function. We show that in the presence of Wannier obstructions, such zeros are irremovable. That is, no symmetric, gap-preserving deformation of the bulk can return the ingap state to the band continuum. We call these states ring states: their wavefunctions show a node at the impurity site, and their mixed band character is set by minimizing the level repulsion exerted by the bands above and below the gap. In Chern insulators, the band mixing endows occupied ring states with local circulating currents, remnant of a small edge mode surrounding the vacancies. Clusters of vacancies bind ring states that hybridize to form dispersive chiral edge modes, providing a real-space view of bulk-boundary correspondence.

papers.title: Numerical methods and analytic results for one-dimensional strongly interacting spinor gases
papers.summary: One of quantum physics' fundamental, but largely unsolved, problems is the computation of the correlation functions in many-body systems. In this paper we address this problem in the case of one-dimensional spinor gases with repulsive contact interactions in the presence of a confining potential. We take advantage of the fact that in the strong coupling limit, the wavefunction factorizes with the charge degrees of freedom expressed as a Slater determinant of spinless fermions and the spin sector described by a spin chain of Sutherland type with exchange coefficients that depend only on the trapping potential. This factorization is also present in the expressions for the correlation functions. Still, analytical and numerical investigations were hindered by the fact that the local exchange coefficients and the charge component of the correlators are expressed as $N-1$ multidimensional integrals, with $N$ the number of particles, which are notoriously hard to compute using conventional methods. We introduce a new approach to calculating these integrals that is extremely simple, scales polynomially with the number of particles, and is several orders of magnitude faster than the previous methods reported in the literature. This allows us to investigate the static and dynamic properties, temperature dependence, and nonequilibrium dynamics for systems with a larger number of particles than previously considered and discover new phenomena. We show that, contrary to natural expectations, the momentum distribution of strongly interacting trapped spinor gases becomes narrower as we increase the temperature and derive simple determinant representations for the correlators in the spin incoherent regime valid for both equilibrium and nonequilibrium situations.

papers.title: Extreme Suppression of Thermal Conductivity in Monolayer Beryllene
papers.summary: We demonstrate an extreme suppression of thermal conductivity in monolayer beryllene through first-principles solutions of the phonon Boltzmann transport equation. While the fully converged three-phonon calculation predicts a room-temperature lattice thermal conductivity of 154.3 W/(m$\cdot$K), inclusion of four-phonon interactions suppresses it to 10.7 W/(m$\cdot$K), a reduction of more than 90\%. This exceptionally large reduction of the thermal conductivity is amongst the highest reported in two-dimensional materials. The microscopic origin of this breakdown is traced to the strong sensitivity of the low-frequency flexural ZA phonons to four-phonon scattering: mode-resolved scattering rates reveal a pronounced enhancement of ZA scattering, which substantially shortens their lifetimes and suppresses their dominant contribution to heat conduction. Moreover, the temperature dependence of the thermal conductivity changes from $\kappa\propto T^{-0.86}$ to $\kappa\propto T^{-1.38}$ upon inclusion of four-phonon processes. Our results establish $\alpha$-beryllene as an unusually strong case of four-phonon-controlled thermal transport amongst two-dimensional materials. These findings identify selective higher-order scattering of flexural phonons as a key mechanism for controlling thermal transport in strongly anharmonic low-dimensional systems.

papers.title: Two-dimensional Topological Quantum Chemistry and Catalog of Topological Materials
papers.summary: Two-dimensional topological materials host symmetry-protected, disorder-robust edge states cen- tral to quantum technologies. Yet, they remain scarce compared with their three-dimensional coun- terparts. We adapt the topological quantum chemistry formalism to layer groups, and study the band topology of 8,872 entries from the computational materials databases C2DB and MC2D. We find 4,073 topological or obstructed entries, including 905 topological insulators and 1,003 obstructed atomic insulators, greatly expanding the library of such materials in two dimensions. Detailed elec- tronic and topological properties of all materials are compiled into a a Topological 2D Materials Database (2D-TQCDB), and the edge states of selected new materials are studied in detail. Our methodology is implemented in new publicly available programs, designed to study the topology of any non-magnetic monolayer or multilayer material.

papers.title: Interplay of spin-phonon coupling in FeSe with pressure and isoelectronic (S/Te) substitution
papers.summary: In several studies, magnetism has been shown to strongly influence the properties of the iron chalcogenide compound \ce{FeSe}. In our previous work [Phys. Rev. Res. 6(4), 043154 (2024)], we demonstrated how the interplay between spin and orbital degrees of freedom governs the electronic structure and consequently shapes the magnetic phase diagram of \ce{FeSe} under external hydrostatic pressure. However, a comprehensive understanding of the phase diagram also requires investigating the role of lattice degrees of freedom (phonons) and their coupling to magnetism. In the present study, we examine how hydrostatic pressure and isoelectronic substitution affect the magnetic and lattice dynamical properties of \ce{FeSe} using Density Functional Theory calculations. Our lattice dynamics analysis reveals that different phonon modes exhibit distinct dependencies on the local magnetic moment across various magnetic phases. We further identify pressure- and magnetic-moment-dependent dynamical instabilities in specific magnetic configurations, highlighting the intricate coupling between structural and magnetic degrees of freedom in \ce{FeSe}. An investigation of spin-phonon coupling demonstrates the presence of strong magnetoelastic interactions affecting the prominent optical phonon modes: the Fe-derived $B_{1g}$ mode and the Se-derived $A_{1g}$ mode. Finally, we discuss the evolution of spin-phonon coupling under pressure and alloying in the context of its possible implications for emergent phases such as magnetism, nematicity, and superconductivity in \ce{FeSe}.

papers.title: CoS++: Towards More General and Explicit Implementations for Sampling High-Order Feynman Diagrammatic Series
papers.summary: We extend combinatorial summation (CoS) of connected Feynman diagrams to Hubbard mod- els with flavor-dependent propagators and counterterm shifts. The construction combines an interaction-occupancy mask with labels for the open fermion cycle, allowing equivalent endpoint his- tories to be accumulated while retaining the flavor and sublattice information needed by subsequent contractions. In the flavor-dependent version, denoted symmetry-broken CoS (SB-CoS), normal heads carry the cycle flavor and counterterm heads inherit the flavor at their interaction partner. We prove the correctness of the resulting recurrence and introduce terminal readouts that return all nonempty interaction-subset values from a shared circuit, as required by a many-configuration Markov-chain sampler. For three flavors, a second formulation uses determinant polynomials and a local interaction tensor, with connected coefficients extracted by subset recursion or Fourier interpo- lation and a support sieve. Applications to the two-spin honeycomb and three-flavor square-lattice Hubbard models illustrate the treatment of sublattice structure and non-uniform reference shifts.

papers.title: peaks: a Python package for analysis of angle-resolved photoemission and related spectroscopies
papers.summary: The electronic band structure, describing the motion and interactions of electrons in materials, dictates the electrical, optical, and thermodynamic properties of solids. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) provides a direct experimental probe of such electronic band structures, and so is widely employed in the study of functional, quantum, and 2D materials. \texttt{peaks} (\textbf{P}ython \textbf{E}lectron spectroscopy \textbf{A}nalysis by \textbf{K}ing group @ \textbf{S}t Andrews) provides a Python package for advanced data analysis of ARPES and related spectroscopic data. It facilitates the fast visualisation and analysis of multi-dimensional datasets, allows for the complex data hierarchy typical to ARPES experiments, and supports lazy data loading and parallel processing, reflecting the ever-increasing data volumes used in ARPES. It is designed to be run in an interactive notebook environment, with extensive inline and pop-out GUI support for data visualisation.

papers.title: Observation of Altermagnetic Spin Splitting in an Intercalated Transition Metal Dichalcogenide
papers.summary: Altermagnetism is a novel magnetic phase combining characteristics of both antiferromagnetism and ferromagnetic ordering. Despite growing theoretical interest in altermagnetic materials, reports of experimentally verified high Neel temperature layered compounds are limited or remain to be firmly established. Here, we present an angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and density functional theory (DFT) study of Co1/4TaSe2, a compound we identify as a layered altermagnetic material. Magnetic susceptibility measurements confirm type A antiferromagnetic ordering with a Neel temperature of 178 K. Our ARPES measurements reveal an electronic band structure in excellent agreement with DFT calculations, demonstrating clear signatures of altermagnetic spin splitting at the Fermi surface. Furthermore, temperature dependent ARPES reveals a reconstructed valence band structure, with observable band shifts and the closing of energy gaps upon heating above the Neel temperature (TN), consistent with the suppression of altermagnetic order. These findings establish Co1/4TaSe2 as a promising platform for exploring altermagnetic phenomena.

papers.title: Anyon polarons as a window into the competing phases of the Kitaev-Gamma-Gamma-prime model
papers.summary: We investigate the dispersions of anyon quasiparticles in the Kitaev honeycomb spin liquid perturbed by $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ couplings in order to understand phase transitions into competing states through anyon gap-closing instabilities. We demonstrate how anyon gap closings provide a way to understand phase transitions into a plethora of previously identified competing phases---including zigzag, stripy, $120^\circ$, and incommensurate spiral phases---and are in agreement with numerical studies not only on the nature of the phases, but also on the specific critical values of $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ couplings. Remarkably, when the antiferromagnetic Kitaev model is perturbed by a negative $\Gamma$ interaction, we find that the single-vison and fermion gaps remain open while the gap of a magnon-like local boson vanishes. This points to a plausible candidate coexistence regime where long-range magnetic order emerges while fractionalized excitations inherited from the Kitaev spin liquid may persist. The magnetic order can be either stripy antiferromagnetic or incommensurate spiral, depending on the sign of $\Gamma'$.

papers.title: Observation of a Novel Charge Density Wave Superstructure in Monolayer 1T-$VS_{2}$ at Room Temperature and its Evolution in Multilayers
papers.summary: Spontaneous formation of charge density wave (CDW) superstructures in monolayers (MLs) of a two-dimensional (2D) crystal lattice is fundamental in understanding its complex quantum states. We report a successful top-down liquid phase exfoliation and stamp transfer process (LPESTP) to create ML VS\textsubscript{2}, undergoing a CDW transition at room temperature. Using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and electron diffraction (ED), we observed the coexistence of 1T and 2H polymorphic phases in VS\textsubscript{2} at room temperature, and only the 1T phase undergoes CDW transition. We discovered a novel incommensurate CDW superstructure ($\sqrt{7} \times \sqrt{7}$) R19.1\textsuperscript{o} in ML 1T-VS\textsubscript{2}. With an increase in the number of layers, the CDW order changes to a commensurate ($2 \times 2\times 1$) superstructure. Using angle-dependent photoelectron spectroscopy and TEM, we have shown that vanadium atoms self-intercalate as V\textsuperscript{3+} ions in multilayer VS\textsubscript{2} and are responsible for the evolution of the CDW superstructure from the incommensurate ($\sqrt{7} \times \sqrt{7}$) R 19.1\textsuperscript{o} to the commensurate ($2\times2\times1$) order. We also report the observation of novel Moir\'e superlattices in twisted bilayer 1T-VS\textsubscript{2} flakes with trapped CDW superstructure of the monolayer. The density functional theory (DFT) calculation performed on ML 1T-VS\textsubscript{2} show that the observed ($\sqrt{7} \times \sqrt{7}$) R 19.1\textsuperscript{o} CDW superstructure has lower energy compared to that of the pristine undistorted ML and the CDW instability is driven by formation of strong soft-phonon modes. Our findings provide an important platform for understanding the evolution of CDW superstructures in 1T-VS\textsubscript{2} with layer numbers and V self-intercalation.

papers.title: Collective dynamics of trail-interacting particles
papers.summary: Trail interactions occur when past particle trajectories bias future motion, rendering the system out of thermodynamic equilibrium. While such systems are abundant in nature, their understanding is limited to the single-particle level or phenomenological mean-field theories. Here, we introduce a minimal model of many trail-interacting particles, which extends this paradigm to the fluctuating collective level in arbitrary dimension. Particles diffuse while depositing long-lasting repelling/attracting trails that act as a shared memory field, coupling their dynamics across time and space. Using stochastic density functional theory, we derive fluctuating hydrodynamic equations and analyze analytically and numerically the resulting behaviors. We show that memory, coupled with fluctuations, fundamentally reshapes collective dynamics; In the repulsive case, the particle density displays superdiffusive spreading for $d=1$ and diffusive spreading for $d\geq2$, characterized by transient clustering and ballistic motion; In the attractive case, the system condensates in finite time into frozen, localized states. Our results establish general principles for trail-interacting systems and reveal how persistent fields generate novel instabilities and drive self-organization.

papers.title: Field-angle-resolved heat transport in UTe$_2$: determination of nodal positions in the superconducting order parameter
papers.summary: One of the recurring hurdles in studying unconventional superconductivity is the challenge of efficiently and conclusively identifying the symmetry of the superconducting order parameter in a new material. Uranium ditelluride (UTe$_2$) exhibits an unprecedented number of superconducting phases as a function of pressure and magnetic field, each presumably characterized by a different symmetry of the superconducting gap function. None of these phases has had its symmetry conclusively identified so far. In this article, we report results of an extensive study of the thermal conductivity of UTe$_2$ in its low-field, low-temperature superconducting state as a function of the angle of an applied magnetic field rotated in the $b$-$c$ plane. We observe clear and substantial oscillations in the thermal conductivity as a function of field angle, which naturally suggests the existence of point nodes in the gap. Utilizing the experimentally determined Fermi surface, we are able to model this phenomenon for all the potential gap structures in UTe$_2$ and positively identify the location of these nodes as being along the crystallographic $b$-axis, implying that the superconducting order parameter belongs to the $B_{2u}$ irreducible representation of the crystal point group. The clarity of this result will accelerate the identification of other superconducting phases in UTe$_2$, and guide future studies through the use of high resolution field-angle-dependent measurements.

papers.title: Fano profile in the resonance fluorescence spectrum of a solid-state quantum emitter coupled to phonons
papers.summary: We present a theory of resonance fluorescence (RF) of a solid-state quantum emitter in the regime of weak optical excitation. The emitter is coupled to the phonon modes of the surrounding bulk semiconductor, described by a super-Ohmic spectral density. We show that the RF spectrum of this system consists of a central elastic line, a broad phonon sideband known from other linear and non-linear spectra of such systems, and a narrow inelastic contribution characteristic of scattering spectra, stemming from noise-induced transient dynamics. At moderate phonon couplings or low temperatures, the interplay between the broad sideband and the inelastic feature leads to a Fano-like profile near the resonant energy with the Fano parameter determined by laser detuning. In the weak-coupling limit (where only single-phonon processes are included), the spectrum becomes an exact Fano shape, with the inelastic component vanishing completely at the exact laser frequency. The amplitude of this spectral feature grows linearly with temperature, while its width depends solely on the spontaneous emission rate of the emitter. Because the spectral line shape is extremely sensitive to dephasing, resonance fluorescence can serve as a direct, non-interferometric probe of coherence at dephasing rates critical for generating highly indistinguishable single photons. We relate the quantum character of the reservoir to the non-commutativity of noise observables and show that the Fano resonance persists in the classical (commutative) limit. We also discuss how the redistribution of optical coupling efficiency between the central line and the sidebands affects the total scattering rate under various excitation conditions.

papers.title: Geometry-Enforced Topological Chiral Fermions in Amorphous Chiral Metals
papers.summary: Since the prediction and observation of topological Weyl semimetals (chiral TSMs), there have been enormous efforts to characterize further condensed matter realizations of chiral fermions. These efforts were dramatically accelerated by the subsequent discovery of a profound link between low-energy topological and lattice chirality in structurally chiral crystals. Though TSMs are well understood in the limit of perfect translation symmetry, real solid-state materials host defects and disorder, and may even be rendered amorphous down to all but the smallest system length scales. Previous theoretical studies have concluded that chiral TSMs transition into trivial diffusive metals at moderate disorder scales, raising concerns that chiral TSM states may only be accessible in highly crystalline samples. In this work, we in contrast identify large families of chiral TSMs that instead persist under strong structural disorder even into the amorphous regime. We show that amorphous chiral TSM phases can be stabilized in particular by the presence of long-range order in the local structural chirality. We present extensive analytic and numerical calculations demonstrating the existence of both Weyl and higher-charge chiral fermions in amorphous metals whose topology and spin and orbital angular momentum textures are tunable via the interplay of average symmetry and geometry. To distinguish and generate new realizations of strongly disordered chiral fermions, we introduce an analytic approach grounded in symmetry group theory. We then introduce an amorphous Wilson loop numerical method to identify chiral fermions in metals with 3D structural disorder. Our findings bridge the crystalline and strongly disordered regimes of chiral TSMs, and indicate a clear route toward engineering geometry-enforced topology in noncrystalline materials and metamaterials.

papers.title: Sound Wave in the Backreaction Affected Spacetime in Analogue Gravity Based on Number-Conserving Approach
papers.summary: Adopting a number-conserving approach, we show that the sound wave in the backreaction-affected dynamical spacetime obeys the equations of motion for a massive scalar field in an analogue spacetime. Even with backreaction, the analogue metric has the same form as that without backreaction, except that the sound velocity, fluid density, and fluid velocity incorporate small corrections that account for backreaction. Moreover, the modification of the classical fluid-dynamical equations by backreaction introduces a spacetime-dependent mass. We also present a linear form of the modified Bogoliubov-de Gennes equation with number conservation, which allows us to solve it numerically. Using a finite-size homogeneous quasi-one-dimensional Bose gas as an example, we find that backreaction enhances the canonically normal-ordered correlation function at the same point, by about $10\%$ in the bulk and up to about $20\%$ near the edges. The bulk enhancement persists when the finite imaging resolution of cold-atom experiments is taken into account.

papers.title: Higher-order response theory in optimal stochastic thermodynamics
papers.summary: Linear response theory has found many applications in statistical physics. One of these is to compute minimal-work protocols that drive nonequilibrium systems between different thermodynamic states, which are useful for designing engineered nanoscale systems and understanding biomolecular machines. We clarify the relationships between linear-response-based approximations used to study optimal protocols in different driving regimes by demonstrating how they arise from a truncation of a causal response, or Volterra, series expansion. We then construct higher-order response terms and discuss the utility and drawbacks of their inclusion in the determination of work-minimizing protocols. We focus on the cases of an overdamped particle in a harmonic trap, and a double well system modeled as a two-state discrete system, ultimately showing that while the inclusion of higher-order response in work approximations can improve predictions of excess work and modestly improve the resulting higher-order optimal protocols, a significant computational expense is incurred while introducing the possibility of predicting arbitrarily low and unphysical negative excess work.

papers.title: Quantum Geometric Entropy Production and Entropy Hall Effect
papers.summary: Quantum geometry has been extensively linked to charge, spin, orbital, and thermal transport in crystalline solids, but its imprint on entropy transport remains largely unexplored. Here we develop a quantum theory of entropy transport for Bloch electrons under an electric field. {Within the relaxation-time approximation, we show that the leading and subleading contributions to entropy production reproduce the Joule heating relation, with the former arising from the linear Drude current and the latter from the nonlinear Drude current and the intrinsic nonlinear Ohmic current. Microscopically, near topological Dirac band crossings and anticrossings, these contributions are controlled by the quantum metric and the fully symmetrized quantum metric dipole, respectively. We further predict a Berry-curvature-induced entropy Hall effect, which, together with the local heat Hall current, provides a simple way to recover the modern theory of orbital magnetization.} Finally, we derive general relations between entropy and charge currents, offering a practical route to probe entropy flow experimentally.

papers.title: Controlling inertial active Brownian motion via stochastic resetting
papers.summary: Inertia is intrinsic to many living and synthetic active systems, from animals and robotic agents to colloidal swimmers, and it strongly shapes transport. Many such systems employ intermittent restart protocols to regulate exploration. Stochastic resetting provides a theoretical framework for these strategies and a route to control nonequilibrium steady states, yet the role of inertia in reset-controlled active dynamics remains poorly understood. Here we study an inertial active Brownian particle in two dimensions under complete and partial stochastic resetting. We derive exact stationary second- and fourth-order scalar moments for the different protocols wherever their stationary limits exist, and obtain the full transient evolution of the mean-squared velocity and displacement under complete resetting. Under complete resetting, inertia strongly enhances localization: at large reset rates, the steady-state mean-squared displacement decays as $r^{-3}$, rather than following the overdamped scaling $r^{-1}$. Kurtosis-based phase diagrams reveal strongly non-Gaussian position and velocity statistics, including activity-induced re-entrant behavior as a function of reset rate and inertia. The transient solutions show that resetting shifts the velocity-relaxation rates, whereas the terminal relaxation of the displacement is governed solely by the mean resetting time $1/r$, with inertia controlling the faster transient modes. Comparing complete resetting with the partial protocols, we find that resetting the velocity together with the position substantially enhances localization. Resetting the orientation to a fixed or a random direction drives the mean-squared velocity toward opposite limits. These results establish inertia, reset frequency, and the choice of reset variables as coupled control parameters for localization, relaxation, and non-Gaussian fluctuations in active systems.

papers.title: Finite-temperature superfluid depletion of disordered Bose gases
papers.summary: At zero temperature, homogeneous interacting Bose-condensed fluids are entirely superfluid, with remarkable transport properties. A non-superfluid, normal component is induced by finite temperatures and spatial inhomogeneity, the combined effects of which are rather intriguing, and difficult to describe quantitatively. We obtain finite-temperature disorder corrections to the normal fraction known since Laudau's seminal two-fluid theory, using diagrammatic perturbation theory for systems of any dimensionality, with closed analytical expressions to leading, quadratic order in disorder strength.

papers.title: On the upper critical dimension of the KPZ universality class: KPZ and related equations on a fully connected graph
papers.summary: We investigate the infinite-dimensional limit of nonequilibrium surface growth by numerically integrating stochastic growth equations on a fully connected graph. In particular, we study the Edwards-Wilkinson (EW), Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ), and tensionless KPZ (TKPZ) equations. Using a network discretization adapted to the all-to-all interaction topology, we analyze the global roughness, height-fluctuation statistics, time power spectra, and two-time correlations. For the EW equation, we obtain an exact expression for the roughness that matches the numerical simulations and shows that the interface becomes flat as the number of nodes in the graph, $N$, tends to infinity. We also compute analytically the time power spectrum, show that height fluctuations are Gaussian, and derive an explicit expression for the two-time height autocorrelation function, indicating that the aging behavior is trivial. For the KPZ equation, finite-size and strong-coupling effects can cause deviations from EW behavior at moderate system sizes $N$, often accompanied by numerical instabilities; however, these differences disappear as $N$ increases. In the large-$N$ limit, KPZ dynamics converges to EW behavior, as the four observables analyzed exhibit identical scaling properties. Overall, our results indicate that on a fully connected graph the KPZ nonlinearity is irrelevant as $N\to\infty$, leading to EW-like dynamics with asymptotically flat interfaces. These findings are interpreted in the context of the upper critical dimension of the KPZ universality class.

papers.title: Active fluctuations drive inertia-free absolute negative mobility in soft and living matter
papers.summary: Absolute negative mobility (ANM) is one of the most paradoxical transport phenomena in which a setup moves on average in a direction opposite to the applied force. The simplest system exhibiting this effect in minimal one-dimensional dynamics involves an inertial particle subjected to a constant bias while dwelling in a nonlinear, symmetric periodic potential in a nonequilibrium, nonstationary state generated by external driving. The necessity of inertia poses a significant conceptual barrier in predicting the ANM in a microscopic world of soft and living matter such as biological cells. In this work, we solve a two-decade old puzzle and demonstrate that none of the previously thought factors required for this effect are decisive. We show that the ANM may occur in a system composed of an overdamped particle in a piecewise linear symmetric periodic potential in an equilibrium state, provided that it is additionally driven by active fluctuations in the form of white Poisson shot noise. Our result may help to explain exotic transport behaviour emerging in biological cells where dynamics is typically overdamped and assisted by active fluctuations derived from various metabolic activities. It can also be exploited for effective separation strategies in a microscopic world, thus transforming fluctuations from a nuisance into a functional resource.

papers.title: Gap structure and phase diagram of twisted bilayer cuprates from a microscopic perspective
papers.summary: Since the prediction of a time-reversal symmetry breaking (TRSB) $d+id^\prime$ state in twisted bilayer cuprate superconductors by Can et al. (Nat.Phys. 17,519(2021)), several experiments have attempted to detect this state, yielding conflicting results. At present, it is not clear which differences in samples or experimental conditions might explain these discrepancies. In this work, we perform a tight-binding lattice model calculation with phenomenological interlayer tunneling, examining the order parameter as a function of twist angle, interlayer tunneling, doping, and temperature. We observe the TRSB state to be correlated to the position of the Van Hove singularity in the normal state, which changes not only as a function of doping but also the tunneling strength. Two such phases are identified as nominally consistent with in-plane $d+id'$ and $d+is$ order, but with unexpected transformation properties under bilayer symmetry operations. We calculate the Josephson critical current, in particular examining the angle dependence for various tunneling strengths. Finally, we discuss the existing experiments in the context of our results.

papers.title: Topologically quantized macroscopic attractor states in hydrated DNA
papers.summary: Driven dissipative systems at ambient conditions typically exhibit continuous responses shaped by fluctuations and relaxation, with discrete macroscopic states arising only under specific dynamical constraints. Here, we report the emergence of discrete attractor states in a quasi-two-dimensional hydrated DNA sample under magnetic excitation. The transverse polarization voltage $V_{xy}$ displays telegraph switching between well-defined levels, indicating stochastic transitions between metastable macroscopic states. Statistical analysis of the voltage time series reveals bimodal distributions and strong Bayesian model selection in favor of multiple coexisting states. A phenomenological phase-field framework describes the observed metastability and switching in terms of a proposed collective $U(1)$ polarization phase. Within this interpretation, phase-slip dynamics and integer-labeled winding sectors provide a possible organizing principle for the discrete macroscopic response. The results suggest that macroscopic quantization can emerge in a classical system at ambient conditions as a consequence of dissipative dynamics constrained by phase topology.

papers.title: Fundamental problems in Statistical Physics XIV: Lecture on Correlation and response functions in statistical physics
papers.summary: In the first part of these short lecture notes, we will present an introduction on (auto-)correlation functions and linear-response functions in the language of a physicist. In particular, the fluctuation-dissipation theorem in classical physics is presented underlining the central role of correlation functions. The fundamental importance of (auto-)correlation functions raises the natural question on how they are characterized in general without referring to the concrete underlying dynamical laws. Perhaps unexpectedly -- despite being elegant and long established in the mathematical literature (Bochner's theorem for correlations; Herglotz-Nevanlinna representations for response) -- this answer is not widely appreciated in physics, partly because the requisite tools lie outside the standard curriculum. In the second part we adopt a more rigorous viewpoint: we state the key structural properties of correlation functions and provide selected derivations of these results. Finally, we return to linear response and discuss general characterization results for response functions.

papers.title: Unambiguous characterization of in-plane dielectric response in nanoconfined liquids: water as a case study
papers.summary: The in-plane dielectric constant of nanoconfined water has attracted growing interest in recent years. Nevertheless, assigning a bulk-like dielectric constant to a molecularly thin film is convention dependent because it requires choosing an effective water width. We propose the in-plane 2D polarizability, $\alpha_{\parallel}$, as a macroscopic characterization of the in-plane dielectric response that avoids this choice. Using classical molecular dynamics simulations, we compute $\alpha_{\parallel}$ via two independent and consistent methods: based on fluctuation--dissipation theory, and from the induced dipole moment when water is placed in a capacitor. papers.title: Double circular dichroism high harmonic spectroscopy: An ultrafast probe for topological photocurrents
papers.summary: Understanding optical responses of topological matter is central to optoelectronic applications, photocurrent control, and spectroscopy. Yet schemes for sensing ultrafast photocurrents and separating bulk and surface contributions are lacking. We introduce double circular dichroism (DCD) harmonic spectroscopy as an all-optical probe of ultrafast dynamics in topological materials. Pump and probe pulses are circular with independently controlled helicities, yielding the circular dichroism of the circular dichroism: a time-resolved response that evaluates how probe-induced dichroism depends on pump helicity. While DCD vanishes in symmetric systems, it survives in broken time-reversal-symmetry materials, including Chern insulators. Simulations in a Haldane nanoflake, where a pump manipulates chiral current-carrying states and intense probe pulses drive harmonic emission, show that DCD arises from bulk and edge-localized states with opposite signs, similar magnitudes, and different amplitude scaling. Edge-associated DCD is connected to the outermost atomic layer of exponentially localized protected modes and is relatively robust to bulk-edge interference, enabling separation of bulk and edge photocurrents. Varying the electronic structure and laser parameters reveals harmonic anomalies that may probe topological attributes of photocurrents and material phase. In particular, HHG DCD oscillations under band-structure manipulation vary strongly across the phase transition and become stable and nonoscillatory in topologically trivial phases. DCD also oscillates with pump-probe delay on attosecond timescales, offering an ultrafast probe of topological photocurrents and their coherence. DCD could therefore disentangle bulk and boundary photoresponses in broken-symmetry quantum and topological matter and be implemented in photoelectron and absorption pump-probe spectroscopies and chiral systems.

papers.title: Crystal-Field Symmetry Constraints in Layered Honeycomb ErBr$_3$
papers.summary: Crystal-field symmetry restricts the ground-state Kramers doublet of ErBr$_3$ to one of two classes. We show that the compressed octahedral environment selects the class with $\langle \psi_\pm | J^{\pm} | \psi_\mp \rangle = 0$, suppressing the lowest-order $J^{\pm}$-mediated exchange. Thermodynamic measurements reveal two zero-field anomalies at 0.375 and 0.200 K. Under an in-plane magnetic field, the thermodynamic response separates into a phase boundary and a broader crossover line. Inelastic neutron scattering measurements at 2 K reveal no well-defined low-energy dispersive magnetic modes. These results connect the ground-state symmetry with the field-dependent thermodynamic response of ErBr$_3$, providing a microscopic starting point for understanding its low-energy magnetic behavior.

papers.title: Femtosecond tunneling spectroscopy of ultrafast band bending dynamics at the atomic limit
papers.summary: Atomic-scale disorder shapes the potential energy landscape traversed by photocarriers, while the carriers themselves also dynamically reshape this landscape. However, resolving ultrafast photocarrier motion at atomic length scales has remained a central challenge in materials science. Here, we demonstrate that lightwave-driven terahertz scanning tunnelling microscopy (THz-STM) provides access to these dynamics by probing the ultrafast evolution of local electronic structure following resonant interband excitation. We introduce a generalized inversion protocol that reconstructs the time-dependent differential conductance directly from measured THz-STM data, enabling quantitative analysis of the photoexcited electronic structure without prior knowledge of the sample's properties. Applying this approach to the photoexcited GaAs(110) surface, we image the resulting femtosecond carrier dynamics by tracking the transient photocurrents produced by ultrafast shifts in the energy alignment of surface and bulk electronic states near individual surface defects. The reconstructed dynamics reveal time-dependent band bending induced by the photocarriers and highlight three key mechanisms that contribute to the ultrafast tunnel current response. Critically, terahertz time-domain sampling of the tip near-field, which both captures the waveform and demonstrates its invariance under sample photoexcitation, allows the intrinsic sample dynamics to be disentangled from the coherent sub-cycle dynamics induced by the terahertz driving field. We establish a new regime of ultrafast tunnelling spectroscopy that captures transient electronic structure and dynamic band alignment with unprecedented spatio-temporal resolution, which has significant implications for understanding carrier transport, defect-mediated processes, and the development of optoelectronic technologies based on dynamically tunable materials.

papers.title: Discrete Lattice Models for Interface Growth on a Complete Graph
papers.summary: We investigate the behavior of discrete interface growth models belonging to the Edwards--Wilkinson (EW) and Kardar--Parisi--Zhang (KPZ) universality classes, when defined on a complete graph, a topology commonly used to probe the infinite-dimensional limit of statistical mechanical systems. Our aim is to assess to what extent discrete lattice models reproduce the behavior of their corresponding continuum equations in this highly connected setting. After assessing the trivial behavior shown by some well known cases (like random deposition with surface relaxation or the etching model), we focus on two paradigmatic models associated with the KPZ universality class, the Restricted Solid-on-Solid (RSOS) and Ballistic Deposition (BD) models, and assess non-trivial behavior through several observables including the roughness, height fluctuations, power spectra, and two-time autocorrelation functions. Still, despite similarities with continuum equations, important differences arise in the fluctuations and long-time dynamics. In both discrete models the rescaled height fluctuations display a pronounced left tail, indicating the presence of lagging nodes. While the RSOS model exhibits a saturation roughness that decreases with system size, similarly to the EW and KPZ equations, the BD model exhibits a saturation roughness that increases with system size and an additional ultrafast growth regime, placing it outside the KPZ universality class on a complete graph.

papers.title: Boundary-dependent topological degeneracy in an Ising chain
papers.summary: The influence of boundary conditions on bulk properties is generally expected to vanish in the thermodynamic limit. Here we show that this expectation can fail in an open transverse field Ising chain with modified boundary fields. By removing only the transverse fields acting on the two edge spins while leaving the bulk Hamiltonian unchanged, we uncover a boundary-induced switching of the topological spectral degeneracy. In contrast to the conventional open chain, where the topological degeneracy occurs in the ferromagnetic phase ($\left\vert g\right\vert 1$). We demonstrate that the underlying mechanism originates from two exact local conserved quantities associated with the edge spins, which partition the Hilbert space into invariant sectors. Based on this structure, we establish an exact description in terms of domain-wall excitations, under which the Hamiltonian decomposes into two independent Kitaev chains. Complementarily, the Majorana representation reveals that the spectral switching originates from different unit-cell conventions and boundary terminations of the corresponding effective SSH lattice, leading to distinct boundary zero-mode structures without altering the bulk Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we show that the boundary-induced topological degeneracy remains observable at finite temperatures through non-Hermitian quench dynamics, providing a dynamical manifestation of the bulk-boundary correspondence. These results demonstrate that boundary engineering, through the introduction of local conserved boundary degrees of freedom, provides an effective route for controlling topological degeneracy in quantum spin chains without modifying bulk interactions.

papers.title: Disorder-driven symmetry suppression by van der Waals planar defects in a magnetic topological insulator
papers.summary: Magnetic topological insulators offer a platform to control electronic topology through magnetic order, yet reliable routes to tune their properties remain limited. Here, we show that ion irradiation allows to modify the magnetic properties and the anomalous Hall response of the van der Waals magnetic topological insulator MnBi$_2$Te$_4$. Using noble gas ion beams, intrinsic defects are introduced via collision cascades without chemical doping. We identify two distinct regimes. At low fluence, cation antisite disorder leads to a near-complete redistribution of Bi over cation sites while preserving long-range crystallographic order, accompanied by a transition from $p$-type to $n$-type transport. At high fluence, cation-anion intermixing drives the formation of a previously unreported layer-disordered phase characterized by a high density of van der Waals-specific planar defects, including swapped bilayers. Despite significant structural disorder, the system retains partial periodic order up to high displacement levels. Magnetometry and X-ray spectroscopy show that the Mn high-spin state and intralayer antiferromagnetic interactions likely persist, while macroscopic magnetic anisotropy is strongly reduced. At the same time, the magnitude of the anomalous Hall conductivity is reduced by an order of magnitude, far exceeding the change in magnetization, and its sign is modified. The observations are consistent with a suppression of the Berry curvature of the occupied states. These results establish ion irradiation as a means to tune anomalous Hall conductivity in topological insulators through defect engineering and reveal a disorder-driven approach to control symmetry and electronic structure in van der Waals magnetic materials.

papers.title: Quantum critical collapse of a pinned vortex glass in high-field superconducting resonators
papers.summary: The interplay between disorder and vortex--vortex interactions in strongly disordered superconductors in a magnetic field can stabilize a vortex-glass state, characterized by strong pinning and the absence of positional order. Yet its role in the destruction of superconductivity at the field-driven superconductor--insulator transition has remained unresolved. Here we use plasmonic microwave spectroscopy of superconducting resonators patterned from amorphous indium oxide thin films to directly track the superfluid density up to the critical field $B_c$. We find an unexpected resilience of the superfluid density, which decreases only logarithmically over nearly three orders of magnitude in field, in stark contrast to the rapid power-law suppression expected for vortex lattices. We attribute this anomalously slow decay to a collective vortex-pinning mechanism counterintuitively enhanced by vortex--vortex interactions. The superfluid density then vanishes linearly at $B_c$, where independent magnetoresistance measurements identify a continuous quantum critical point, unlike the abrupt transition observed at zero field. We further uncover an exceptionally large nonlinear electromagnetic response of the vortex glass, manifested as a pronounced positive-Kerr effect with potential for quantum sensing. These results show how disorder controls the critical magnetic field and identify the vortex glass as the key intermediate state governing the magnetic-field-induced superconductor--insulator transition.

papers.title: Nambu Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics and the Lyapunov Structure of Open Systems
papers.summary: We investigate the thermodynamic meaning of the dissipation potential in Nambu nonequilibrium thermodynamics (NNET) using a simple open-piston model. The system is described by three variables: the gas volume, the piston momentum, and the thermodynamic entropy of the gas. The reversible dynamics is formulated in terms of two Nambu Hamiltonians, the extended energy and the thermodynamic entropy, while the irreversible dynamics is generated by a bath-relative Massieu-type dissipation potential through a positive-semidefinite gradient flow. This construction reproduces the physical processes of frictional heating and heat exchange with the reservoir while preserving their thermodynamic interpretation. We show that the time derivative of the dissipation potential coincides with the total entropy production rate of the system and the heat bath. Although the subsystem entropy may evolve nonmonotonically, the dissipation potential is a Lyapunov function under the conditions realized in this model. These results provide an explicit thermodynamic interpretation of the dissipation potential and its associated Lyapunov structure within NNET.

papers.title: Thermal Signatures of the Slater-Mott Crossover in the Hubbard Model: From Double Occupancy to Antiferromagnetic Correlation Length
papers.summary: The interaction-driven crossover from a Slater insulator to a Mott insulator in the N\'{e}el-ordered ground state of the Hubbard model is a fundamental paradigm of strongly correlated electrons, yet its quantitative characterization has remained elusive. Here we establish a clear and experimentally accessible thermal criterion for this crossover via the sign change of the temperature derivative of double occupancy, $(\partial D/\partial T)_U$, near zero temperature. In the Slater regime, $(\partial D/\partial T)_U>0$ reflects the major role of charge fluctuations; in the Mott regime, the anomalous $(\partial D/\partial T)_U<0$, a manifestation of the Pomeranchuk effect, signals the dominance of low-energy spin superexchange physics. Using exact diagonalization and {\it numerically exact} quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that this criterion determines the crossover boundary at $U_{\rm cross}/t=4.0(2)$ for the half-filled two-dimensional Hubbard model. Furthermore, we obtain a consistent boundary independently from the maximum in the antiferromagnetic correlation length, which also arises from the superexchange physics. These two thermal signatures are theoretically unified through the local minimum of thermal entropy versus interaction $U$ at low temperatures. Our results offer a direct, measurable, and physically intuitive framework to identify the Slater-Mott crossover in optical lattice experiments.

papers.title: Electron state tomography from quasiparticle interference maps
papers.summary: Characterizing electronic band structures requires precise knowledge of wave functions and their quantum geometry. Here, we introduce a tomography method to reconstruct the density matrix of electron states from quasiparticle interference maps around single impurities. We consider two-orbital models on a honeycomb lattice, relevant to graphene heterostructures and direct-gap semiconductors. For on-site impurities, backscattering between time-reversed states directly maps the density matrix populations and coherences into distinct orbital contributions in the interference map. While local probes usually lack orbital resolution, these orbital contributions transform under distinct symmetry group representations and can thus be disentangled to reveal the density matrix and quantum geometric tensor of the scattering states. This establishes impurities as tomographic probes for band structures in scanning tunneling microscopy using conventional, unpolarized tips.
